543\n\n--- Page 10 ---\nPreface\nMost individuals today are more conscious of their environment than in\nthe past and they are interested especially in those factors that degrade the\nenvironment. Mining is one of those factors. Mining refers to the process\nofextraction or abstraction of mineral deposits from either the surface of the\nEarth or from beneath the surface. In this context it also involves the abstrac-\ntion of oil, gas, water and brine from the ground. Furthermore, mining repre-\nsents one of man’s earliest activities reaching back into Palaeolithic times and,\nas such, has played an important role in the development of civilization. It is\nalso an activity that has and is going on more or less worldwide. With time,\nthe use of minerals has increased in both volume and variety in order to meet\na greater range of purposes and demand by society. Accordingly, present day\nsociety is more dependent on the minerals industry than in the past. Indeed,\nthe exploitation of minerals is fundamental to society now and will continue\nto be in the future. In other words, the mining of minerals contributes to the\nsustained economic progress of developed nations and helps to alleviate\npoverty and improve the quality of life of people in developing countries.\nFirst, mineral deposits have to be located, they then are worked and\nsubsequently processed. It is the working and processing of mineral\ndeposits that can give rise to environmental damage. This can mean that\nland is disturbed, that the topography is changed\n\n--- Page 11 ---\nx Preface\nbe assessed more readily. As such, it is hoped that this book will be of value\nto those who are involved with the development or redevelopment of min-\ning areas. Although it has been attempted to give a broad overview of the\nsubject this, no doubt, has been influenced by the experience of the authors\nso that it may reflect a certain bias. Case histories have been provided at the\nend of each chapter, except that of the Introduction. These generally illus-\ntrate the content of the individual chapter but in someinstances go further\nand introduce new material. Numerous references have been provided to\nhelp allow the reader to pursue his/her interests further.\nAs far as the authors are aware, there is no book available today that is\nsimilar to this in content. In other words, no book provides a survey, in par-\nticular, of various aspects of subsidence, of waste disposal, of pollution and\nof dereliction as caused by different types of mining, and their investigation\nand treatment. In addition, topics such as spontaneous combustion, gases\nand induced seismicity also are included within the text. Nonetheless, not\nevery aspect of environmental degradation such as noise and \n\n--- Page 12 ---\nChapter 1\nIntroduction\n1.1. Introduction\nMining, alongside agriculture, represents one of man’s earliest activities, the\ntwo being fundamental to the development and continuation of civilization.\nIn fact, the oldest known mine in the archaeological record is the Lion Cave\nin Swaziland, which has a radio carbon age of 43000 years. There\nPalaeolithic humans mined hematite, which they presumably ground to\nproduce the red pigment ochre. Moreover, the dependence of primitive\nsocieties on mined products is illustrated by the terms Stone Age, Bronze\nAge and Iron Age, a sequence of ages that indicate the increasing complex-\nity of the relationship between mining and society. In order to produce a\nflint axe meant that a suitable deposit of flint had to be located, that a\nmethod of mining be developed that would allow the flint to be worked,\nand that a means of processing be evolved to fashion the flint into a finished\nproduct. These requirements are more or less the same for mineral produc-\ntion at the present time. This general sequence applied in the Bronze and\nIron Ages but the processing in particular became more sophisticated. With\ntime, the use of minerals has increased in both volume and variety in order\nto meet a greater range of purposes and demand by society, and the means\nof locating, working and processing minerals has increased in complexity.\nToday, society is even more dependent on the minerals industry than in the\npast. In fact, it can be claimed that every material thi\n\n--- Page 13 ---\n2 Introduction\nthat it is a robber economy, in that a mineral deposit is a finite resource and\nso mining comes to an end when the mineral deposit is exhausted or\nbecomes uneconomic to mine or abstract. Perhaps groundwater abstraction\nis the exception in that with proper management it should be sustainable.\nDeposits that are abandoned when they become uneconomic to work may\nbe reworked at some time in the future when mining technology or demand\nmakes their exploitation once again worthwhile.\nMining, and associated mineral processing and beneficiation, does\nimpact on the environment. Unfortunately, this frequently has led to\nserious consequences. The impact of mining depends on many factors,\nespecially the type of mining and the size of the operation. It can mean that\nland is disturbed, that the topography is changed and that the hydro-\ngeological conditions are affected adversely. Mining also has social impacts\non the environment. Communities grow up around mines. When the mines\nclose, the communities can suffer and even may die, becoming ‘ghost\ntowns’.\nIn the past the mining industry frequently showed a lack of concern for\nthe environment. This does not necessarily imply that society was not aware\nof the environmental problems that could be associated with mining. For\ninstance, in 1306 a royal proclamation prohibited the use of coal in London\nfor domestic and industrial purposes because of the nuisance caused by\nsmoke but it proved impossible to enforce. In addition, Agricola\n\n--- Page 14 ---\nIntroduction 3\nhowever, are a local phenomena, although they may impact beyond\nmine boundaries. They also account for only a small part of the land area\nof a country (e.g. the mining industry accounts for less than 1% of the total\narea of South Africa). Land that has become derelict by past mining activ-\nity can be reclaimed. Rehabilitated spoil heaps frequently become centres of\nsocial amenity such as parklands, golf courses and even artificial ski slopes.\nOpen-pits, when they fill with water, can be used as marinas, for fishing or\nas wildlife reserves. Environmental problems and impacts\nMining may be regarded as the removal of minerals, in solid, liquid or\ngaseous form, from the Earth’s crust for use in the service of society.\nIttherefore involves exploration for and exploitation of mineral deposits by\nsurface or underground methods. Accordingly, mining inevitably brings\nabout change to the environment and so has an environmental impact. The\ndegree of impact can vary from more or less imperceptible to highly intru-\nsive and depends on the mineral worked, the method of working, and the\nlocation and size of the mine. Unfortunately, there is no consistent means\nby which to quantitatively assess some environmental impacts, notably\nthose of a visual nature, so that any assessment of such impact tends to be\nqualitative with an appreciable element of subjectivity. On the other hand,\nsome impacts can be quantitatively assessed such as the degree to which\ngroundwater has been polluted. Obviously, the most severe environmental\nimpacts occur where mining is going or has gone on, the effect of the impact\nreducing with increasing distance from the mine responsible.\nMining can pose a direct hazard to humans, apart from mine employees.\nFortunately, mining hazards only infrequently lead to death or serious\ninjury. Nonetheless, there are instances when, for example, old partially\nsealed shafts have opened beneath people who then have fallen to their\ndeath, where tailings dams have burst and killed people or where spoil h\n\n--- Page 16 ---\nIntroduction 5\nObviously, the larger the size of a mining operation, the larger the impact\nis likely to be since it will produce more waste, occupy more land and have\na greater number of buildings and plant.\nThe extent to which mining becomes an environmental impact depends\nto a large extent upon the number of people that a mine affects. Frequently,\ncommunities grow up around mines and so have to live with many of the\nenvironmental problems that are consequent on mining. A good example is\nprovided by coal mining. For instance, many of the industrial and urban\nareas of Britain developed on coal fields (Fig. 1.2). That is not to say that\nmineral exploitation in rural areas does not make an environmental impact.\nFor example, restrictions are placed on quarry or mine development in\nnational parks in Britain because of their amenity and recreational value.\nHowever, the opposition to such development tends to come from those\nwho are not directly involved with mining. Those to whom mining repre-\nsents a source of employment are much less likely to offer objections to the\nexpansion and continuance of their means of livelihood. In developing\nnations even less opposition is forthcoming against the development of min-\ning because it represents a means of employment and hopefully a way of\nraising living standards. Examples \ninclude microorganisms, (e.g., E. coli, Giardia, and noroviruses), inorganic chemicals (e.g., lead, \narsenic, nitrates, and nitrites), organic chemicals (e.g., atrazine, glyphosate, trichloroethylene, \nand tetrachloroethylene), and disinfection byproducts (e.g., chloroform). EPA and the Food and \nDrug Administration (FDA) are both responsible for the safety of drinking water. FDA regulates \nbottled drinking water, while EPA regulates drinking water provided by public water systems. \nEPA sets enforceable drinking water standards for public water systems, and unless otherwise \nspecified, the term “drinking water” in this text refers to water provided by these systems. The \ndrinking water standards include maximum contaminant levels and treatment technique \nrequirements for more than 90 chemical, radiological, and microbial contaminants, designed to \nprotect people, including sensitive populations such as children, against adverse health effects.2,7 \nMicrobial contaminants, lead, nitrates and nitrites, arsenic, disinfection byproducts, pesticides, \nand solvents are among the contaminants for which EPA has set health-based standards. \n\nMicrobial contaminants include bacteria, viruses, and protozoa that may cause severe \ngastrointestinal illness.2 Children are particularly sensitive to microbial contaminants, such as \nGiardia, Cryptosporidium, E. coli, and noroviruses, because their immune systems are less \ndeveloped than those of most adults.8-14  \n\nDrinking water is a known source of lead exposure among children in the United States, \nparticularly from corrosion of pipes and other elements of the drinking water distribution \nsystems.15-17 Exposure to lead via drinking water may be particularly high among very young \nchildren who consume baby formula prepared with drinking water that is contaminated by \nleaching lead pipes.15 The National Toxicology Program has concluded that childhood lead \nexposure is associated with reduced cognitive function, reduced academic achievement, and \nincreased attention-related behavioral problems.18 \n\nFertilizer, livestock manure, and human sewage can be significant contributors of nitrates and \nnitrites in groundwater sources of drinking water.19,20 High levels of nitrates and nitrites can \ncause the blood disorder methemoglobinemia (blue baby syndrome)21-23 and have been \n\nAmerica’s Children and the Environment | Third Edition, Updated October 2015 \n\n1 \n\n\fDrinking Water Contaminants | Environments and Contaminants  \n\nassociated with thyroid dysfunction in children24,25 and pregnant women.24,26,27 Moderate \ndeficits in maternal thyroid hormone levels during early pregnancy have been linked to reduced \nchildhood IQ scores and other neurodevelopmental effects, as well as unsuccessful or \ncomplicated pregnancies.28 \n\nArsenic enters drinking water sources from natural deposits in the earth, which vary widely \nfrom one region to another, or from agricultural and industrial sources where it\n---\n\n=== Clean.pdf ===\nClean Without water, life cannot exist; \nhence this vital resource should not be hampered or polluted. Water is one of \nthe most precious natural assets abound on the earth. Over 70% of the earth \nsurface is covered with water, which is a universal solvent essential for life. \nAll biological processes in cells take place in an aqueous medium; all reactions \nwithin cells between various substances occur between the substances that are \ndissolved  in  water.  The  availability  of  water  is  important  for  deciding  the \nnumber of individuals of each species that can survive in one particular area. \nIt is quite evident that diversity of life in any particular location is very much \ndecided by the availability of water there. Hence, it is an undeniable fact that \nwater is a vital resource because it by itself determines the life on earth. The \nterm 'pollution' generally refers to the addition of any foreign body or deletion \nof anything that naturally exists. Anything that causes hindrance to the usage \nof water by any form of life is termed as water pollution. The polluted water \nis either unsuitable or toxic to the kind of life that is existing in that area. All \nforms  of  life  on  earth  directly  or  indirectly  depend  upon  water  for  their \nsurvival. The major surface of the Earth’s surface is covered by water. All that \nwater exists in nature in various compartments of atmosphere and lithosphere, \nmaking it susceptible to pollution. The sources of water pollution are domestic \ndrainage and sanitary waste, industrial drainage and sewage, industrial waste \nfrom  factories,  dumping  of  domestic  garbage  on  on-land  bodies,  chemical \nrunoff  and  many  others.  Water  can  get  polluted  by  solid  particulates  in \nsuspension  and  also  by  dissolved  species  in  solution.  Pollution  can  be \nmanaged depending on the situation. The agents that cause pollution are called \npollutants.  They  include  organic,  inorganic,  and  biological  entities. Before  the  19th  century  industrial  revolution,  people  lived  in  harmony  with \n\ntheir  immediate  environment.  As  the  industrialization  has  spread  around  the  globe,  the \n\nproblem of water pollution has intensified. Today with over 8 billion people on the planet, the \n\npressure  on  the  water  resources  has  increased  and  water  pollution  has  become  an  emerging \n\nthreat.  In order to combat water pollution we must understand the problems associated with \n\nwater  pollution  and  become  the  part  of  the  solution.  In  this  context  the  course  Aquatic \n\nPollution  and  Coastal  Zone  Management  has  been  designed  to  expose  the  under  graduate \n\nstudents  of  Fisheries  Science  to  various  dimensions  of  Aquatic  Pollution,  resulting \n\nEnvironmental  and  Public  Health  Hazards  and  various  tools  available  for  monitoring  and \n\nabatement  of pollution. In addition,  the coastal ecosystems  which are highly productive and \n\nrich  in  biodiversity  has  been  explained.  The  course  Aquatic  Pollution  and  Coastal  Zone \n\nManagement has been divided into two parts. The first part covers Aquatic Pollution and the \n\nsecond part Coastal Zone Management. \n\nClassification of aquatic pollution \n\nPollution \n\nPollution is  defined as an undesirable  change in  the physical,  chemical  or biological \n\ncharacteristics of the environment, which can harmfully affect the health, survival or activities \n\nof  humans  or  other  living  organisms.  Environmental  pollution  is  an  emerging  threat  and  of \n\ngreat  concern in  today's  context  pertaining to  its effect  on the ecosystem. The technological \n\ndevelopments  in  agriculture,  industries  and  related  fields  have  resulted  in  unlimited \n\nexploitation of natural resources disturbing the delicate ecological balance between the living \n\nand nonliving components of the biosphere. \n\nMarine Pollution  \n\nGESAMP defined marine pollution as \"introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of \n\nsubstances  or  energy  into  the  marine  environment  (including  estuaries)  resulting  in  such \n\ndeleterious effects as harm to living resources, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine \n\n \n\factivities  including  fishing,  impairment  of  quality  for  use  of  sea-water,  and  reduction  of \n\namenities. \n\nGESAMP  (Group  of  Experts  on  the  Scientific  Aspects  of  Marine  Environmental \n\nProtection) is a group of experts that since 1969 has advised the United Nations system on \n\nscientific aspects of marine environmental protection. GESAMP is presently sponsored by ten \n\nUN agencies with interests and responsibilities in marine environmental matters: IMO, FAO, \n\nUNESCO-IOC,  WMO,  IAEA,  UN,  UN  Environment,  UNIDO,  UNDP  and  ISA.  This  joint \n\nadvisory mechanism is needed first to provide a cross-sectoral, interdisciplinary, and science-\n\nbased  approach  to  international  policy  development  in  marine  environmental  affairs,  and \n\nsecond  to  meet  the  practical  requirement  for  coordination  and  cooperation  among  UN \n\nagencies. \n\nPollutant  \n\nPollutant is  a  substance  that  pollutes  the  air,  water  or  land.  This  term  is  used  to \n\ndescribe things in the environment that do not belong. In a broader sense, the term 'pollutant' \n\nhas even been used to  describe undesirable levels of sound or light. Environmental problems and impacts\nMining may be regarded as the removal of minerals, in solid, liquid or\ngaseous form, from the Earth’s crust for use in the service of society.\nIttherefore involves exploration for and exploitation of mineral deposits by\nsurface or underground methods. Accordingly, mining inevitably brings\nabout change to the environment and so has an environmental impact. The\ndegree of impact can vary from more or less imperceptible to highly intru-\nsive and depends on the mineral worked, the method of working, and the\nlocation and size of the mine. Unfortunately, there is no consistent means\nby which to quantitatively assess some environmental impacts, notably\nthose of a visual nature, so that any assessment of such impact tends to be\nqualitative with an appreciable element of subjectivity. On the other hand,\nsome impacts can be quantitatively assessed such as the degree to which\ngroundwater has been polluted. Obviously, the most severe environmental\nimpacts occur where mining is going or has gone on, the effect of the impact\nreducing with increasing distance from the mine responsible.\nMining can pose a direct hazard to humans, apart from mine employees.\nFortunately, mining hazards only infrequently lead to death or serious\ninjury. Nonetheless, there are instances when, for example, old partially\nsealed shafts have opened beneath people who then have fallen to their\ndeath, where tailings dams have burst and killed people or where spoil heaps\nhave failed causing death. Effluents from mines and mine wastes may be\ntoxic and kill vegetation, and injure animals. Water pollution can continue\nfor a long period after the mine causing the problem has ceased operation\nand as such can pose a health hazard. About 21.71% of\nthe country’s geographical area is under forests, which are at a very critical juncture\ntoday. The increasing threats of forest depletion and destruction constitute new\nchallenges to environmental security, biodiversity maintenance, and achieving sus-\ntainable development in the country.\nThis volume, entitled Forest Degradation and Management: An Indian\nPerspective, is particularly timely as the urge to comprehend, evaluate, and counter\nforest degradation has become extremely important. It aims to advocate the integra-\ntion of various aspects of forestry science and practice to represent a more compre-\nhensive view of forest degradation processes and their impacts emerging from\nIndian forests.\nThis compilation, which aims at establishing the preliminary context of the\nIndian forests, begins with a comprehensive description of the causes and processes\nof deforestation and forest degradation and their analysis in space and time. This in\nturn opens the way for examining the more specific causes of these changes that are\ntaking place in the forested areas, which are both man-made and natural. The con-\ntribution of climate change and the role of carbon emissions to local forest degrada-\ntion provide an essential understanding of the global impacts of local processes.\nWhat is most appealing about this volume is the presence of different perspectives.\nThe comparison of these classical and modern evaluation techniques is beneficial to\nboth practitioners and researchers, as it traces the growth of forest monitoring pro-\ncesses. Such technical precision is complemented by a concern for ecology, explor-\ning how such degradation may propagate at the ecosystem level as functional loss,\nbiodiversity erosion, and the breakdown of vital ecosystem services. Managing\nIndian forests requires addressing soil health issues as well as forest degradation. A\nfocused study of herpetofauna in the Western Ghats biodiversity hotspot makes a\ncompelling argument about how forest degradation quickly impacts specific taxo-\nnomic groups. The forest regeneration impacts reveal the impacts of forest over-\nstress on the outlook of our forest ecosystems.\nv\n\n--- PAGE 7 ---\nvi Preface\nA significant strength of this volume is its emphasis on the integration of scien-\ntific analysis and management aspects. The research findings presented in each\nchapter are based on field research and include practical aspects that may be useful\nto forest managers, policymakers, and conservationists. In this manner, the reading\nof the book is constructive as it contributes to both theory and practice of forest\nmanagement in India. This construction comes at a time when India is focusing on\nits commitment to steps that would strengthen the cause of conservation and resto-\nration of forests, as indicated in our national objectives of increasing and enhancing\nforest cover and decreasing forest degradation. It is the intention of the authors to\nwrite a book that would be necessary in implementing these aims using logic and\nmanagerial approaches.\nTura, Meghalaya, India Gopal Shukla\nGajapati, Odisha, India Abha Manohar K.\nOrono, ME, USA Anil Raj Kizha\nChandigarh, Chandigarh, India Pankaj Panwar\nPundibari, West Bengal, India Sumit Chakravarty\n\n--- PAGE 8 ---\nContents\nPart I Forest Degradation: Assessment\nTrends of Deforestation and Forest Degradation in India\nand Its Impact . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 3\nAbhilash Dutta Roy, Sumit Kumar Das, Gopal Shukla, Pankaj Panwar,\nand Sumit Chakravarty\nDegradation of Forests in India: Causes and Restoration Efforts . . . . . . . . 23\nTara Kumari, Sohom Seal, N. Most of the states\nwith the highest net forest loss are in Northeast India, which is renowned for its rich\nbiodiversity and fragile ecosystems.\nThe repercussions of diminishing forest cover in Northeast India extend beyond\nthe loss of trees; they directly threaten the species that call these forests home,\nincluding the local Indigenous communities. The delicate balance of ecosystems is\ndisrupted, affecting local flora and fauna and, in turn, impacting the livelihoods of\nlocal communities dependent on these ecosystems for sustenance. The increasing\ncultivation of plantation crops such as oil palm, rubber, and areca nut further exac-\nerbates the challenges, signaling a transformation in the traditional way of life for\nthese communities.\n\n--- PAGE 27 ---\n10 A. D. Roy et al.\nFig. 2 The state-wise net forest loss in India between 2000 and 2022\n5 Impact of Anthropogenic Disturbance on Biodiversity\nin Indian Forests\nDeforestation constitutes a primary catalyst for the extinction of biodiversity in\ntropical regions. The ramifications of deforestation within tropical biodiversity\nhotspots are particularly alarming due to the concentration of globally endemic spe-\ncies in these areas. Despite this, there is a dearth of comprehensive documentation\non the effects of extensive deforestation on native biotas in the Himalayan biodiver-\nsity hotspot. India is a treasure chest of biodiversity that hosts many plants and has\nbeen identified as one of the eight primary centers of origin and crop diversity. It\naccounts for 7–8% of the global biodiversity, with an estimated 5150 plant species\nand 1837 animal species as endemic (Venkataraman 2012). Being the center of\norigin of many domesticated species, India’s biodiversity includes wild relatives of\nmany crops and domesticated animals. The country has 16 major types and 251\nsubtypes of forests. As one of the 17 identified megadiverse countries, India has 10\nbiogeographical zones and is home to 9% of the known mammalian species.\nHowever, India has seen a tremendous deforestation rate due to population pres-\nsure in the past centuries and has four biodiversity hotspots: the Himalayas, Indo-\nBurma, Sundaland, and Western Ghats. However, this trend is being seen in other\n\n--- PAGE 28 ---\nTrends of Deforestation and Forest Degradation in India and Its Impact 11\ncountries, too. Globally, the prospects for tropical forests and the biodiversity\ntherein are becoming increasingly bleak, owing to unabated deforestation and forest\nalteration stemming from human activities such as logging, hunting, agricultural\nexpansion, and human settlement (Giam 2017). It was projected that at the current\ndeforestation rate, total forest cover in the Indian Himalayas will be reduced by the\nend of this century to about half of the forest cover as reported in 1970, and the\ndense forests will be reduced to only 34%. According to the extinction theory, larger\nand more specialized species are likely to be lost due to deforestation (Sodhi et al.\n2004). A troubling trend of deforestation has been reported in the Indian Himalayas\nand forecasts the potential extinctions of endemic taxa (species and subspecies) by\nthe year 2100 across diverse taxonomic groups, encompassing gymnosperms,\nangiosperms, fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Considering the\ncurrent magnitude of deforestation, it is projected that by 2100, merely 10% of the\nIndian Himalayas’ land area will be covered by dense forest (>40% canopy cover).\nUnder such circumstances, almost a quarter of the endemic species face the risk of\nextinction, including 366 endemic vascular plant taxa and 35 endemic vertebrate\ntaxa. Additionally, relevant findings underscore the significance of accurate report-\ning of forest cover data by governmental institutions. Inaccuracies in reporting lead\nto underestimations of the biological consequences of deforestation and have the\npotential to result in miscalculations in land-use decisions, such as the construction\nof hydroelectric dams (Pandit et al. 2007). Research indicates that species depen-\ndent on forest ecosystems typically struggle to adapt to habitat loss (Brooks et al.\n2002). Consequently, it is imperative to conserve habitats and prioritize the manage-\nment of species deemed vulnerable to these changes. Urgent and extensive conser-\nvation initiatives are imperative to mitigate the imminent biodiversity losses driven\nby deforestation.\n6 Impact of Overgrazing in the Forests\nof the Indian Himalayas\nGrazing in forests has been shown to significantly impact plant community struc-\nture and diversity. Overgrazing and under-grazing in montane forests have been\nseen to negatively impact vegetation community composition and are in accordance\nwith the intermediate disturbance hypothesis (Kikoti and Mligo 2015). Forest deg-\nradation by overgrazing livestock can significantly impact the ecosystem, particu-\nlarly in loss of pasture biomass and reduction in ecosystem carbon stocks (Eldridge\nand Delgado-Baquerizo 2017).\nIn addition to plant community structure and biomass, grazing impacts soil prop-\nerties and hydrology. Livestock overgrazing has been seen to negatively impact soil\nproperties in montane forests, where livestock grazing decreased the accumulation\n\n\n--- PAGE 29 ---\n12 A. D. Roy et al.\n2015). Selective browsing by animals has also been seen to lead to soil erosion,\ndepressed growth of seedlings and saplings, and reduced recruitment due to tram-\npling (Sharma et al. 2009). Overgrazing and browsing in forests can lead to the\noverconsumption of forage, which can harm the biodiversity and sustainability of\nthe forest ecosystem. However, properly managed, targeted livestock grazing can\nhave benefits, such as increased habitat diversity and regeneration of selected can-\nopy tree species. However, these effects are context-dependent and require further\nresearch (Öllerer et al. 2019). Cattle grazing have positively impacted vegetation\nstructure and dynamics, including germination, seed dispersal, flower and fruit pro-\nduction, and conservation of soil features (Mazzini et al. 2018).\nIndia’s cattle density is around 62 heads per km2 compared to the global average\nof 10 heads per km2 (Robinson et al. 2014). In the Himalayas, uncultivated fodders\nare an integral component of farming systems in the hills, with grass-dominated\nrangelands showing a good fodder value (Singh and Bohra 2005; Singh et al. 2008).\nThe region’s forests contribute significantly to the livestock sector in rural house-\nholds and have implications for policy planning for poverty alleviation (Pandey\n2011). However, rapidly growing livestock and human populations and unrestricted\novergrazing have led to a decline in the density of vegetative cover in India. The\nincreasing numbers of livestock can be attributed to the fact that the Indian Green\nRevolution had little impact on livestock production, and livestock pressure is a\nsignificant cause of forest degradation (Holden and Sankhayan 1998). In the Central\nHimalayas, the human population has been doubling every 27–30 years (Samal\net al. 2003). As a result, it has been seen that the current forest fodder extraction rate\nis likely to be unsustainable (Pandey et al. 2014). Heavy grazing has reduced spe-\ncies diversity, increased the occurrence of ruderal and weedy species, and inhibited\nthe regeneration of tree species (Kala and Rawat 1999; Thakur et al. 2011). The\nregular collection of fodder from the forests has been an essential factor in causing\nsoil erosion, low fertility of the land, and other degradation processes in the hill\nareas (Chandra et al. 2008). Grazing has been seen to have altered the forest cover,\naffecting soil moisture regimes in the Sikkim Himalayas (Prokop and\nPłoskonka 2014).\nThe unavailability of fodder from other sources in the Himalayas may be the\nreason for the degradation of forest areas because these are more frequently used\nand are vital for the existing farming systems (Pandey et al. 2014). The strategy for\nreducing forest degradation must revolve around providing alternative fodder\nsources to the community for livestock rearing while encouraging the protection of\nthe forest cover. Agroforestry can be a potential strategy to enhance climate change\nresilience among smallhol\n\n--- PAGE 30 ---\nTrends of Deforestation and Forest Degradation in India and Its Impact 13\nfor sustainable forest management can help strengthen the local economy and\nthereby help reduce dependence on fodder for livestock.\n7 Impact of Anthropogenic Disturbance on Mangrove\nForests of India\nMangrove forests provide many ecosystem services and functions, including but not\nlimited to timber and various NTFPs such as tannins, wax, honey, and aquaculture.\nThey also boast vibrant soil organic carbon (SOC) pools sequestered up to ten times\nmore blue carbon than above-ground pools. Mangroves are rich-blue carbon pools,\nwith a global above- and below-ground carbon stock of mangrove forests of 1.6\nPega grams (Pg) and 10.2 Pg, respectively (Kauffman et al. 2020). These plants also\nplay a significant role in climate change adaptation by stabilizing coastal lands\nthrough their complex structure and in areas that permit landward accretion of\norganic buildup, significantly reducing the impact of sea level rise. The dependence\nof coastal people on mangrove forests for direct use due to the scarcity of alternate\nresources may cause these fragile ecosystems to become highly disturbed. These\ninclude resource extraction, such as fuelwood consumption (Ambastha et al. 2010),\nand the expansion of shrimp monoculture (Datta and Deb 2017; Kumar 2012). The\nimpact of these anthropogenic activities on land use change further exacerbates the\nloss of mangroves (Kumar 2012).\nIndia lost 428 km2 or 8.4% of its mangrove forests between 1980 and 2009\n(Dasgupta and Shaw 2013). From 1975 to 2005, approximately 75 km2 of Indian\nmangroves have been converted for aquaculture, and 171 km2 for agriculture (Giri\net al. 2008). For example, in the Bhitarkanika mangrove of Odisha, there was a\nsignificant extraction of resources such as fuelwood despite the forest being a pro-\ntected area (Ambastha et al. 2010). In the Indian Sundarbans of West Bengal, the\ncomposition of significant mangrove species such as Heritiera fomes and Excoecaria\nagallocha have witnessed a decline of about 10% from 1977 to 2015, mainly due to\nanthropogenic factors such as overexploitation of timber (Ghosh et al. 2016). The\nmangrove forests in the Indian Sundarbans have suffered a lot owing to forests\nbeing converted for agriculture (Dasgupta and Shaw 2013). In the mangroves of\nMaharashtra, urbanization and industrialization have been identified as the main\ndrivers of anthropogenic impacts (Mugade and Sapkale 2014).\nTo ensure the resilience of mangrove forests against anthropogenic pressure, col-\nlaborative efforts between government bodies, forest fringe local communities, and\nenvironmental organizations are necessary. Community engagement and strict\nenforcement of regulations are crucial components of any effective solution.\nMangroves managed by nongovernmental organizations collaborating with local\nforest dependents have previously shown good performance (Datta 2018).\nParticipation of forest-dependent communities in forest resource ma\n\n=== END L-0025804346-pdf.pdf ===\n\n=== START book.pdf ===\nTotal pages: 535\n--- PAGE 1 ---\nhttp://www.nap.edu/catalog/989.html\nWe ship printed books within 1 business day; personal PDFs are available immediately.\nBiodiversity\nE.O. The biosphere is an intricate tapestry of interwoven life\nforms. Even the seemingly desolate arctic tundra is sustained by a complex interaction of\nmany species of plants and animals, including the rich arrays of symbiotic lichens. The\nbook before you offers an overall view of this biological diversity and carries the urgent\nwarning that we are rapidly altering and destroying the environments that have fostered the\ndiversity of life forms for more than a billion years.\nThe source of the book is the National Forum on BioDiversity, held in Washington,\nD.C., on September 21–24, 1986, under the auspices of the National Academy of Sciences\nand Smithsonian Institution. The forum was notable for its large size and immediately\nperceived impact on the public. It featured more than 60 leading biologists, economists,\nagricultural experts, philosophers, representatives of assistance and lending agencies, and\nother professionals. The lectures and panels were regularly attended by hundreds of\npeople, many of whom participated in the discussions, and various aspects of the forum\nwere reported widely in the press. On the final evening, a panel of six of the participants\nconducted a teleconference downlinked to an estimated audience of 5,000 to 10,000 at\nover 100 sites, most of them hosted by Sigma Xi chapters at universities and colleges in\nthe United States and Canada.\nThe forum coincided with a noticeable rise in interest, among scientists and portions\nof the public, in matters related to biodiversity and the problems of international\nconservation. I believe that this increased attention, which was evident by 1980 and had\nsteadily picked up momentum by the time of the forum, can be ascribed to two more or\nless independent developments. The first was the accumulation of enough data on\ndeforestation, species extinction, and tropical biology to bring global problems into\nsharper focus and warrant broader public exposure. It is no coincidence that 1986 was also\nthe year that the Society for Conservation Biology was founded. The second development\nwas the growing awareness of the close linkage between the conservation of biodiversity\nand economic development. In the United States and other industrial countries, the two\nlanigiro\neht\nmorf\nton\n,koob\nrepap\nlanigiro\neht\nmorf\ndetaerc\nselif\nLMX\nmorf\ndesopmocer\nneeb\nsah\nkrow\nlanigiro\neht\nfo\nnoitatneserper\nlatigid\nwen\nsihT\n:elif\nFDP\nsiht\ntuobA\n,deniater\neb\ntonnac\n,revewoh\n,gnittamrof\ncificeps-gnittesepyt\nrehto\ndna\n,selyts\ngnidaeh\n,skaerb\ndrow\n,shtgnel\nenil\n;lanigiro\neht\not\neurt\nera\nskaerb\negaP\n.selif\ngnittesepyt\n.noitubirtta\nrof\nnoisrev\nevitatirohtua\neht\nsa\nnoitacilbup\nsiht\nfo\nnoisrev\ntnirp\neht\nesu\nesaelP\n.detresni\nyllatnedicca\nneeb\nevah\nyam\nsrorre\ncihpargopyt\nemos\ndna\nBiodiversity\nhttp://www.nap.edu/catalog/989.html\nv\nCopyright © National Academy of Sciences. But in the developing nations, the opposite is true.\nDestruction of the natural environment is usually accompanied by short-term profits and\nthen rapid local economic decline. In addition, the immense richness of tropical\nbiodiversity is a largely untapped reservoir of new foods, pharmaceuticals, fibers,\npetroleum substitutes, and other products.\nBecause of this set of historical circumstances, this book, which contains papers from\nthe forum, should prove widely useful. It provides an updating of many of the principal\nissues in conservation biology and resource management. It also documents a new alliance\nbetween scientific, governmental, and commercial forces—one that can be expected to\nreshape the international conservation movement for decades to come.\nThe National Forum on BioDiversity and thence this volume were made possible by\nthe cooperative efforts of many people. O.*1, Omotayo, O. E.2, Olatubi, I. V.2, Ogungbile, P. O.1, Asifat, J. T.3, and\nOyebamiji, V.O.3\n1Environmental Management and Crop Production, College of Agriculture, Engineering and Science,\nBowen University, Iwo, Nigeria\n2Pure and Applied Biology Programme, College of Agriculture, Engineering and Science,\nBowen University, Iwo, Nigeria\n3Department of Geography, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife\nReceived: 9/8/2021 Accepted: 2/10/2021\n© Unit of Environmental Studies and Development, Aswan University\nAbstract:\nOne of the challenges that pose threats to human survival in these contemporary times is\nenvironmental degradation. The over-exploitation of natural resources is currently at an alarming\nrate in developing nations with an unabated population increase like Nigeria and may continue to\nspell hardship and discomfort if efforts are not made by all stakeholders to checkmate the trend.\nThe rate at which the human population is increasing also needs to be checked in order to ensure\nsustainable availability of environmental resources for both present and unborn generations. The\ncontrol is necessitated to ensure that the natural resources such as soils, water, forest, mineral\nresources amongst others are sustainably utilized for human survival. This review therefore\nexamines the subject matter of degradation in the tropical environment, its remote causes,\nconsequences in order to proffer measures for checkmating the trend. The planet Earth remains\nthe only one in the universe that accommodates life in abundance, and so, all stakeholders in\nenvironmental management and other related professions need to put in necessary efforts through\nwhich the degradation of the Earth resources may be curtailed.\nKeywords: Degradation; Environment; Developing Nations; Natural Resources; Tropics\nIntroduction\nMan’s Perception of Environment: Ancient and Contemporary times\nThe term ‗environment‘ first appeared in the early 17th century and was coined from a\nFrench word, ―environia‖ meaning act or fact surroundings (Xu, 2017). Since then, the concept\nhas passed through changes and usage, and is still changing since about 1910, but enormous\nshifts in the concept usage and definition were more prominent in the 1920s, 1970s and 2000s.\nToday, the term environment has become a household concept being used quite often to achieve\nhuman targets, especially in ensuring human survival and sustenance.\n_____________________________\nCorresponding author*: E-mail address: timothy.ogunbode@bowen.edu.ng\nPage 218 Ogunbode et al., 2021\n\n--- Page 2 ---\nAswan University Journal of Environmental Studies (AUJES) 2 (4), pp. 218-239, (2021).\nOnline ISSN: 2735-4237, Print: ISSN 2735-4229. https://aujes.journals.ekb.eg/\nIn the light of this fact, Xu (2017) submitted that the concept of environment has not only\nbecome more and more abstract, but also abides in people‘s ideologies and serves as a tool in\nsocio-political movements toward realizing a particular targets in human history.\nIn the 19th century the content of this term started changing. In the early 19th century, the\nterm environment was extended from the surroundings to the more abstract and complex life\ncircumstances through Carlyle‘s translation of Goethe‘s work, and it later was endowed with a\nnew concept of organism-environment interaction through Spencer‘s Principles of psychology in\nthe mid-nineteenth century and it got popularized since the late 19th century (Xu, 2017). The\nadjective term, ―environmental‖, first appeared in literature in 1887 while in 1923, the term was\ncoined to ―emphasizing on environment in the development of an individual or group‖. By 1972,\nthis subject matter was further developed and referred to as ―the ecological sense of living\nthings”. It is referred to both abiotic and biotic environment.\nFrom a historical perspective in the Nigerian context, forested areas within the country\nwere seen as sacred environments or areas that man should not just tamper with or encroach into\nespecially without conducting a form of appeasement to the local gods. Thus, these forests\nharboured the presence of several shrines for worshipping deities or gods which the local people\nbelieved to be the power residing in such forests (Babalola, 2011). Adesiji and Babalola (2012)\nreported that thickly forested zones were believed to be areas that should be preserved and or\nprotected and safeguarded to the maximum for their sacredness. Thus, in most traditional\nsettlements, many places covered with trees were regarded as no-go areas. Such places were\ngiven such names as igbo aiwo (which means forest no one should not dare to enter among the\nYoruba tribe in the southwestern part of Nigeria. Apart from this, most forests found along rivers\nare places of worship of gods in some communities. For instance, Osun deity is worshipped in the\nforested zone along Osun River, Igbo Oro and Odoje worshippers stationed close to Oba River\namong the Yoruba people (Babalola, 2011;).\nSome other ancient and ornamental items at times are being kept within the forested\nplaces in some areas. For instance, Oranmiyan Staff (Opa Oranmiyan) is kept within the tree\ncovered areas in Ile-Ife, Nigeria. In addition, masquerade worshippers among the Yoruba tribe\ndesignated a forested area where Oro (another deity) and the bigger masquerades stay until the\nsmaller ones come out to showcase their strength (Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada,\n2000). With the growing trend of increased urbanization and population explosion, most of our\nnatural forests and environment in t\n\n--- Page 3 ---\nAswan University Journal of Environmental Studies (AUJES) 2 (4), pp. 218-239, (2021).\nOnline ISSN: 2735-4237, Print: ISSN 2735-4229. https://aujes.journals.ekb.eg/\nOkotoni (2004) corroborated the view of the World Bank report when he broadly\nconsidered environment as the totality of natural and human surrounding and activities including\nbiophysical components and processes of the natural environment of land, water and air,\nincluding all layers of the atmosphere, all inorganic and organic matters, both living and non-\nliving, socio-economic components and processes of the human environment including social,\neconomic, technological, administrative, cultural, historical, archaeological, land and its\nassociated resources. Though, several research have revealed that land degradation has its causes\n(for example, Maingwa et al., (2007), it has been equally discovered that the menace inflicts\nexternal or off-site costs which also impacts harder on the society. These impacts are, however\ndifficult to evaluate because they are indirect, non-marketed and even difficult to trace (Barbier,\n1998). In view of this, this investigation becomes imperative to examine the subject matter of\ndegradation in the tropical environment, its causes, consequences in order to sensitize all\nstakeholders to the challenge and to proffer measures for checkmating the trend in order to ensure\nsustainable living on earth. The planet Earth remains the only one in the universe that\naccommodates life in abundance, and so needs to be protected by all.\nTheoretical Background to explanation of Land Degradation\nThree theories prominently used in environmental economics are often adopted to explain\nthe concept of land resource degradation. These are social cost theory, collective good theory and\nthe theory of property rights all of which are closely related to the concept of externality. The\nconcept of externality refers to situations when the effect of production or consumption of goods\nand services imposes costs or benefits on others which are not reflected in the process charged for\nthe goods and services being provided. Example of externalities include water pollution,\ndeforestation, soil erosion, climate change among others (Centemeri ,2009; Spash, 2021). The\nconcept of negative externality of which land degradation is one, according to neoclassical\neconomists can only be resolved by creating markets for environmental goods to curtail further\ndeterioration of the resource (Centemeri ,2009).\nHowever, from the perspective of the theory of social cost according to Pigou (1920), it is\nargued that land degradation results from farmer‘s agricultural practices for which they do not\nbear the full costs, whether negative or positive externalities that cannot be transformed into\nincome and force land users to adopt inappropriate production practices (Wachter, 1992).\nThe second theory, theory of collective goods shares some similarities with social cost since\nexterns, according to Wachter, (1992)\n\n--- Page 4 ---\nAswan University Journal of Environmental Studies (AUJES) 2 (4), pp. 218-239, (2021).\nOnline ISSN: 2735-4237, Print: ISSN 2735-4229. https://aujes.journals.ekb.eg/\nmotivation to take required responsibility of the resource/s, they possess no moral justification to\nto utilize the resource in a socially optimal way (Wachter, 1992; Hazell and Lutz, 1999).\nEnvironmental Degradation and its Perceptions\nChopra (2016) defined environment as the physical surrounding of man/woman of which\nhe/she is a part of and on which is dependent for his/her activities like physiological functioning,\nproduction and consumption. In addition, he defined environmental degradation as the\ndisintegration of the earth or destruction of the environment through the consumption of assets\nlike air, water and soil. Degradation means to bring down the grade of a resource (Lund, 2009).\nFor instance, the stream water could be as of high quality as man wants it but with the\nintroduction of particles of different kinds and qualities, the quality grade of the water changes to\nthe extent that its direct consumption poses threat to human life. Similarly, soils in a natural\nenvironment will continue to maintain its quality as long as it remains undisturbed. Once any\nother externality is introduced into the location/environment, there is distortion in the status and\nthe integrity of the resource, even when such externality seems to have a positive influence on the\noutput of the resource the long run effect of the introduced material is degradation of the resource\n(Maurya et al., 2020). For example, the use of chemical fertilizer may seem productive but it\nleads to the loss of the fertility status of the soil. In the long run, other features of environmental\ndegradation include disfigurement of the land surface, aesthetic degradation like scenic\ndegradation, disruption of biodiversity and deforestation with attendant ecological effects (Savei,\n2012).\nEzeaku and Davidson (2008) defined land degradation (a variant of environmental\ndegradation) as the loss of utility or potential utility through the reduction or damage to physical,\nsocial, cultural, or economic features and/or reduction of ecosystem diversity. It is also the\ntemporary or permanent decline in the productivity of the land. What constitutes a degradation of\nthe environment is a contemporary description of our natural environment. The first worldwide\ndiscussion on issues relating to the environment was held at United Nations Conference in\nStockholm in 1972 with 114 nations in attendance. Babalola (2011) noted that the initial\nenvironmental value seems to be depreciating and, apart from the loss of value and benefits\nderivable from it, there are adverse effects of the loss of value.\nThe word ‗degradation‘, means to ‗lose grade‘ or ‗to fail to perform up to the initial\nlevel‘. Thus, water becomes degraded if it could not be freely used for the same purpose it had\nserved or could not serve the coverage it used to. Also, the air becom\n\n--- Page 5 ---\nAswan University Journal of Environmental Studies (AUJES) 2 (4), pp. 218-239, (2021).\nOnline ISSN: 2735-4237, Print: ISSN 2735-4229. https://aujes.journals.ekb.eg/\ndammed surface water that is able to serve 250 km2 at inception but over time could no longer\nserve the entire area again could be attributed to anthropogenic and natural effects which have led\nto the degradation of the dam environment. The causes of the degradation could be multifarious\nincluding increased sedimentation of the dam as a result of surface erosion (the event which may\nlead to reduced water volume of the reservoir); it could be as a result of the removal of vegetation\nin the vicinity of the dam environment, farming activities and aging trees could all contribute to\nthe degraded value of the dam. A similar scenario is peculiar to soil resources.\nFigure 1: Land badly degraded for human sustainability (Source: Google image)\nA forested soil that formerly provides various forest resources for human use may become\ndegraded as a result of deforestation, large scale agricultural practices (both crop production and\nanimal grazing) to the extent that such resources could not meet up the demand and needs of that\ncommunity. In which case, the community has to seek substandard alternatives. Thus, the\nreplacement of hardwoods such as Iroko, Mahogany, Obeche, with fruit trees such as mango tree,\nkola nut tree or coconut tree is enormous and obvious signs of a degraded environment. Many\nother resources in the environment are all susceptible to degradation if not preserved and\nconserved sustainably.\nb) Numerical Coverage: Environmental degradation could also be viewed in terms of the ability\nof the environment to serve the number which it served at inception or at the beginning (usually\nreferred to as natural stage or undisturbed stage). Natural resource may be overstressed if it is\nused to serve more community than what it was designed for; thus becoming degraded because of\nits excessive use or overuse. By illustration, a dug-out well that serves a community at inception,\nif when degraded could not serve the community again as a result of distortion in the quality\nstatus of the resource. An environment becomes degraded when the land resources initially\nsufficiently used for agriculture without any crisis becomes a source of trouble for that\ncommunity. Nigeria has been seriously facing the challenge of degradation in the past decades as\nfarmers and herdsmen have been clashing over land resource. Herdsmen, in course of searching\nfor pastures for their animals encroach into farms and consequently inflicting destruction on the\ncrops. The much reported crises between farmers and herdsmen is a testimony of vast\ndegradation of the Nigerian environment, most especially in the middle belt, south western and\nsouth eastern part regions of the country. Perhaps this is understandable because soil's capacity to absorb pollutants has masked their long term effects. Unfortunately, this has meant that much of the legislation and regulation that does mention soil is actually designed to protect our water or air environment rather than soil for its own sake. \nBut at last this is set to change. \nSoil degradation is a global problem. A recent report by the European Environment Agency and the UN Environment Programme concludes there are 150 million hectares of European soils at high risk from erosion and that up to one-third of soils may be significantly degraded. The most serious problems, it suggests, are building works that take soil out of productive use, erosion, slope stability, contamination, acidification, desertification in central and eastern Europe, and large data gaps which hamper decision-making. \nThe forthcoming Sixth European Environmental Action Plan includes an objective to protect soils from pollution and erosion and proposes a soil protection strategy. It is likely that a Framework Directive will be formulated specifically for soil. All of this provides an international context for SEPA's recommendation for a Scottish soil protection strategy and a framework within which regulation and legislation can be integrated to give our soils the protection they deserve. \nKen Collins \nChairman \n2 \nScotland has a large diversity of soil types that react in different \nways to environmental pressures. There are few parts of the country that escape the \npressures that we inflict on our soil, whether from air pollution, agricultural and forestry practices, including applying waste to land, or from industrial contamination. \nThere are nearly 12,000 hectares of derelict and vacant land, mostly in and around our towns and cities. Rosen  \nReceived: 16 November 2014 / Accepted: 27 February 2015 / Published: 25 March 2015 \n \nAbstract:  Soil degradation in India is estimated to be occurring on 147 million hectares \n(Mha) of land, including 94 Mha from water erosion, 16 Mha from acidification, 14 Mha from flooding, 9 Mha from wi nd erosion, 6 Mha from salinity, and 7 Mha from a \ncombination of factors. This is extremely serious because India supports 18% of the OPEN ACCESS\nSustainability 2015 , 7 3529 \n \n world’s human population and 15% of the worl d’s livestock populati on, but has only 2.4% \nof the world’s land area. Despite its low proportional land area, India ranks second \nworldwide in farm output. Agriculture, forestry , and fisheries account for 17% of the gross \ndomestic product and employs about 50% of the total workforce of th e country. Recommendations  included  a \ncomprehensive  strategy  involving  sustainable  behaviors,  strict  laws,  and  advanced  treatment \ntechnology.  The  study  emphasized  the  need  for  governments,  companies,  and  communities  to \nwork  together  to  implement  strong  legislation,  improve  infrastructure,  and  increase  knowledge \nabout  water  quality.  Addressing  these  challenges  requires  a  holistic  approach,  focusing  on \nmitigating constraints through ongoing research, innovation, and international collaboration. \n\n_____________________________________________________________________________________________________ \n\n*Corresponding author: E-mail: najmaldin.hassan@uoz.edu.krd; \n\nJ. Examples \ninclude microorganisms, (e.g., E. coli, Giardia, and noroviruses), inorganic chemicals (e.g., lead, \narsenic, nitrates, and nitrites), organic chemicals (e.g., atrazine, glyphosate, trichloroethylene, \nand tetrachloroethylene), and disinfection byproducts (e.g., chloroform). EPA and the Food and \nDrug Administration (FDA) are both responsible for the safety of drinking water. FDA regulates \nbottled drinking water, while EPA regulates drinking water provided by public water systems. \nEPA sets enforceable drinking water standards for public water systems, and unless otherwise \nspecified, the term “drinking water” in this text refers to water provided by these systems. The \ndrinking water standards include maximum contaminant levels and treatment technique \nrequirements for more than 90 chemical, radiological, and microbial contaminants, designed to \nprotect people, including sensitive populations such as children, against adverse health effects.2,7 \nMicrobial contaminants, lead, nitrates and nitrites, arsenic, disinfection byproducts, pesticides, \nand solvents are among the contaminants for which EPA has set health-based standards. \n\nMicrobial contaminants include bacteria, viruses, and protozoa that may cause severe \ngastrointestinal illness.2 Children are particularly sensitive to microbial contaminants, such as \nGiardia, Cryptosporidium, E. coli, and noroviruses, because their immune systems are less \ndeveloped than those of most adults.8-14  \n\nDrinking water is a known source of lead exposure among children in the United States, \nparticularly from corrosion of pipes and other elements of the drinking water distribution \nsystems.15-17 Exposure to lead via drinking water may be particularly high among very young \nchildren who consume baby formula prepared with drinking water that is contaminated by \nleaching lead pipes.15 The National Toxicology Program has concluded that childhood lead \nexposure is associated with reduced cognitive function, reduced academic achievement, and \nincreased attention-related behavioral problems.18 \n\nFertilizer, livestock manure, and human sewage can be significant contributors of nitrates and \nnitrites in groundwater sources of drinking water.19,20 High levels of nitrates and nitrites can \ncause the blood disorder methemoglobinemia (blue baby syndrome)21-23 and have been \n\nAmerica’s Children and the Environment | Third Edition, Updated October 2015 \n\n1 \n\n\fDrinking Water Contaminants | Environments and Contaminants  \n\nassociated with thyroid dysfunction in children24,25 and pregnant women.24,26,27 Moderate \ndeficits in maternal thyroid hormone levels during early pregnancy have been linked to reduced \nchildhood IQ scores and other neurodevelopmental effects, as well as unsuccessful or \ncomplicated pregnancies.28 \n\nArsenic enters drinking water sources from natural deposits in the earth, which vary widely \nfrom one region to another, or from agricultural and industrial sources where it is used as a \nwood preservative and a component of fertilizers, animal feed, and a variety of industrial \nproducts.29 Population studies of health effects associated with arsenic exposure have been \nconducted primarily in countries such as Bangladesh, Taiwan, and Chile, where arsenic levels in \ndrinking water are generally much higher than in the United States due to high levels of \nnaturally occurring arsenic in groundwater.30 Long-term consumption of arsenic-contaminated \nwater has been associated with the development of skin conditions and circulatory system \nproblems, as well as increased risk of cancer of the bladder, lungs, skin, kidney, nasal passages, \nliver, and prostate.29,31 In many cases, long-term exposure to arsenic begins during prenatal \ndevelopment or childhood, which increases the risk of mortality and morbidity among young \nadults exposed to arsenic long-term.32 A review of the literature concluded that epidemiological \nstudies of associations between exposure to arsenic and some adverse health outcomes \npertinent to children’s health have mixed findings. These include studies of associations \nbetween high levels of exposure to arsenic and abnormal pregnancy outcomes, such as \nspontaneous abortion, still-births, reduced birth weight, and infant mortality, as well as \nassociations between early-life exposure to arsenic and increased incidence of childhood cancer \nand reduced cognitive function.33  \n\nWater can contain microorganisms such as parasites, viruses, and bacteria; the disinfection of \ndrinking water to reduce water-borne infectious disease is one of the major public health \nadvances of the 20th century.34 The method by which infectious agents are removed or \nchemically inactivated depends on the type and quality of the drinking water source and the \nvolume of water to be treated. Surface water systems are more exposed than groundwater \nsystems to weather and runoff; therefore, they may be more susceptible to contamination.4,35 \nSurface an\n\n--- LAST 3000 CHARS ---\n Coli) Final Rule. \n 54 \n(124):27544-68. \n\nTotal Coliform Rule: Basic Information\n\n88. Hence, extensive toxicological\nstudies need to be carried out. There is a paucity of regulatory standards on various classes of\nECs. In many countries, there are no proper regulations on ECs due to shortage of\ntoxicological data. In India, the drinking water standards include the regulatory standards for\nonly a few pesticides in the Indian Standards (IS 10500). The water treatment plants and\nWWTPs are not monitored for the presence of ECs. World Health Organisation (WHO) has\npublished extensive regulatory standards for several classes of ECs. The European Union\n(EU) Water Framework Directive has listed 45 priority compounds with environmental\nquality standard to be adhered in aquatic environments. The United States Environmental\nProtection Agency (USEPA), under the Safe Drinking Water Act regulates the ECs listed on\nthe Contaminant Candidate List (CCL) which have been detected in the public water system\nand has not yet been regulated. The USEPA regulates at least five contaminants from the CCL\nevery five years. It is also required to issue a new list of not more than 30 unregulated\ncontaminants to be monitored by public water systems every five years. The\nconcept of externality refers to situations when the effect of production or consumption of goods\nand services imposes costs or benefits on others which are not reflected in the process charged for\nthe goods and services being provided. Example of externalities include water pollution,\ndeforestation, soil erosion, climate change among others (Centemeri ,2009; Spash, 2021). In addition, he defined environmental degradation as the\ndisintegration of the earth or destruction of the environment through the consumption of assets\nlike air, water and soil. Degradation means to bring down the grade of a resource (Lund, 2009).\nFor instance, the stream water could be as of high quality as man wants it but with the\nintroduction of particles of different kinds and qualities, the quality grade of the water changes to\nthe extent that its direct consumption poses threat to human life. Similarly, soils in a natural\nenvironment will continue to maintain its quality as long as it remains undisturbed. Once any\nother externality is introduced into the location/environment, there is distortion in the status and\nthe integrity of the resource, even when such externality seems to have a positive influence on the\noutput of the resource the long run effect of the introduced material is degradation of the resource\n(Maurya et al., 2020). For example, the use of chemical fertilizer may seem productive but it\nleads to the loss of the fertility status of the soil. In the long run, other features of environmental\ndegradation include disfigurement of the land surface, aesthetic degradation like scenic\ndegradation, disruption of biodiversity and deforestation with attendant ecological effects (Savei,\n2012).\nEzeaku and Davidson (2008) defined land degradation (a variant of environmental\ndegradation) as the loss of utility or potential utility through the reduction or damage to physical,\nsocial, cultural, or economic features and/or reduction of ecosystem diversity. It is also the\ntemporary or permanent decline in the productivity of the land. What constitutes a degradation of\nthe environment is a contemporary description of our natural environment. Forest Survey of India, an organization under the\nMinistry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, has been mandated to carry\nout a regular assessment of forest resources of the country using satellite data and\nfield based information and publish the results in a biennial report named as India\nstate of Forest Report (ISFR). The first report was published by FSI in 1987 and since\nthen 17 such reports have been published by FSI. The ISFR 2023 is 18th in the series.\nThe information on various forestry parameters given in the ISFR are very useful for\nmonitoring of the resources, evaluation of the various polices and making better\nplanning for optimum utilization of the forest resources. In addition, the inputs\ngiven in the report are very useful for monitoring of NDC targets, reporting of Green\nHouse Gas (GHG) inventory to UNFCCC for the forest land under the LULUCF sector,\nand country reporting to FAO for the Global Assessment of Forest Resources.\nThe first major input that goes into the ISFR is forest cover mapping of the\ncountry based on nationwide forest cover mapping using satellite data. The forest\ncover is defined as “all lands, more than one hectare with a tree canopy density\nof more than or equal to 10% irrespective of ownership, legal status and land use.\nSuch lands may not necessarily be a recorded forest area. It also includes orchards,\nbamboo and palm”. In the current cycle, Forest Cover Mapping has been carried\nout using medium-resolution indigenous satellite data, with a spatial resolution of\n23.5 m sourced from the Indian Space Research Organization’s (ISRO) indigenous\nLISS-III sensor, part of the IRS Resourcesat satellite series, at a scale of 1: 50,000.\nThis satellite data was acquired for all states within the timeframe of October 2021\nto December 2021. In certain regions of the country, such as the North Eastern\nregion, the coastal belt, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, additional satellite\nimages were procured for the period from January 2022 to April 2022, to obtain\nbetter-quality satellite imagery. This specific time window was chosen because\nit typically offers cloud-free satellite data and full vegetation foliage, resulting in\nenhanced reflectance and precise satellite image interpretation.\n\nxiii\n\nThe classification of forest cover used in the present report is based on tree\ncanopy density, viz., Very Dense Forest (VDF) having canopy density equal to or\nmore than 70%, Moderately Dense Forest (MDF) having canopy density equal to\nor more than 40% but less than 70%, and Open Forest (OF) having canopy density\nequal to or more than 10% but less than 40%.\nThe Forest Cover is assessed using an approach involving satellite digital\nimage processing; visual image analysis; ground verification by the analysts and\nState Forest Departments; incorporation of post-field corrections; quality checks\nForest Survey of India\n\n\fincluding ground validation by officers; followed by generation of output in the\nform of maps and area statistics.\nOver the years, this methodology has continuously evolved and improved\nto keep pace with advancing technology and the latest image interpretation\ntechniques. Since the initial forest assessment report in 1987, the methodology\nfor Forest Cover Mapping has been consistently refined and updated. To ensure\nconsistency, uniformity, and a high level of accuracy in the Forest Cover Mapping\nexercise, all steps of the methodology have been standardized. To minimize\nsubjectivity, a comprehensive manual has been developed to guide and facilitate\nthese processes, helping to maintain the quality and reliability of the mapping\nresults.\nThe second major input that goes into ISFR is based on the inventory of\nForests and Trees Outside Forests (TOF) under the National Forest Inventory (NFI)\nProgramme of FSI. FSI launched a National Forest Inventory in 2002, with the\nonset of the 10th five-year plan, by developing a sampling design, to generate the\nnational level estimates of growing stock and other parameters. Under this NFI\ndesign, the country was stratified into 14 physiographic zones and 60 districts\nwere selected for the detailed inventory for a cycle of 2 years. About 3,500 sample\nplots were inventoried in the forest areas and 5000 sample plots were inventoried\nin TOF every year. FSI modified the sampling design of NFI in 2016, considering\nthe data requirements at National and International level, to generate the precise\nestimates at the State level and to reduce the revisit time from 20 years to 5 years.\nUnder the modified design, FSI has switched over to a grid based design having\nuniform grids of size 5 km x 5 km and selecting specified grids each year for the\ndetailed inventory. Under this design, FSI is laying about 6,000 plots in forest area\nand 10,000 plots in TOF areas every year. The information of growing stock, tree\ncover, bamboo stock, carbon stock, agroforestry and important characteristics are\nderived from the field inventory data collected from forest and TOF.\nThe ISFR 2023 has been produced into two volumes considering the wealth\nof information generated from forest cover mapping and NFI. The report gives comprehensive assessment\nof the forest resources of the country based on interpretation of satellite data and field based\nNational Forest Inventory (NFI). While satellite data gives forest cover, NFI provides Growing Stock\nand Carbon. The data period of the satellite used for this assessment is in general October 2021 to\nDecember 2021 and NFI used for this assessment is 2017-22.\nForest cover mapping/assessment is a biennial exercise in which wall to wall mapping is done\nusing Indian remote sensing satellite data (IRS-LISS III sensor with 23.5 m resolution) as provided by\nNRSC. The report gives information on forest cover of country at state, district, and forest division\nlevel; and changes in forest cover in respect of the previous assessment of 2021. Information on\nforest cover inside and outside the recorded forest area, forest cover in hills districts, forest cover\nin North Eastern States, mangrove is also provided. For the first time, forest cover change matrix\ninside and outside forest areas have been provided separately for clarity in analysis. In the present\nreport, FSI has given forest cover information for 751 districts including those created in the recent\npast, as against 636 districts given in ISFR 2021. Latest district boundaries were received from the\nSurvey of India. In addition, to making the report more relevant to the Divisional Forest Officers,\nwho are the primary administrative heads in forest administration, for the first time Division\nwise forest cover information has also been given for those States from where digitized division\nboundaries were received. FSI has perfected forest cover mapping methods, by enhancing ground\ntruthing (GT). Data of National Forest inventory, as a ready to use KML file, has also been provided\nto the analysts carrying out Forest Cover mapping for improving quality of mapping. Concurrent\nmonitoring of FCM work by supervisors and frequent visits to the field after every few scenes\nimproved the perception of analysts. PDA based application for GT ensured data fidelity.\n\nix\n\nContemporary issues have also been attempted e.g. Forest Cover change in Western Ghats.\nThe report also contains estimates of tree cover, growing stock, carbon stock and important\ncharacteristics of forests derived from the data collected from sample plots spread over the entire\ncountry under NFI. As another first, the trees between 5-10 cm have been included in the analysis\nfor Tree Cover and Growing stock as they are a major contributor to paper and pulp industry.\nBamboo cover has also been estimated for the first time and included in Tree cover. Agroforestry\nhas been analyzed separately as it accounts for 1,27,590 km2 of tree cover and 1,292 M m3 of\nGrowing stock and serves as livelihood enhancer. It has gained further importance due to earning\ncarbon credits in Agroforestry.\nForest Survey of India\n\n\fAn analysis on Forest cover degradation between 2011-2021 has been carried out for identifying\n93,000 km2 potential areas for upgradation of density and additionally sequestering 636 Mt of\nCarbon.\nForest fire alerts has become one of the most important activities of FSI. Pre-Fire alerts, nearreal time alerts are being sent for several years. In the forest fire chapter we have given information\non forest fires in 705 Protected areas for the first time. Similarly Burnt area assessment has been\ndone for the first time at national level and can support course-correction for the policy makers.\nA separate chapter has been given on decadal changes, highlighting changes in forest cover\nand other parameters over a decade. The information given in the report will also be very useful for\nforest planners and to monitor the NDC targets and making policy changes.\nFSI has always endeavored to keep pace with the advancements in tools and technologies, and\nkept the methodology and sampling design of NFI abreast to meet the data requirement of the\nforestry sector both at national and international level. The data processed for the report is also\nused as inputs for GHG inventory of the forest land under the LULUCF sector, and reporting of\ncountry data to FAO for Global Forest Resource Assessment.\nI take this opportunity to express my heartfelt thanks for the continuous support and guidance\nreceived from Shri Bhupender Yadav, Hon’ble Minister, EF&CC; Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh, Hon’ble\nMinister of State, EF&CC; Smt Leena Nandan, Secretary, MoEF&CC, Govt. of India and Shri C.P.
