Forest Survey of India, an organization under the\nMinistry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, has been mandated to carry\nout a regular assessment of forest resources of the country using satellite data and\nfield based information and publish the results in a biennial report named as India\nstate of Forest Report (ISFR). The first report was published by FSI in 1987 and since\nthen 17 such reports have been published by FSI. The ISFR 2023 is 18th in the series.\nThe information on various forestry parameters given in the ISFR are very useful for\nmonitoring of the resources, evaluation of the various polices and making better\nplanning for optimum utilization of the forest resources. In addition, the inputs\ngiven in the report are very useful for monitoring of NDC targets, reporting of Green\nHouse Gas (GHG) inventory to UNFCCC for the forest land under the LULUCF sector,\nand country reporting to FAO for the Global Assessment of Forest Resources.\nThe first major input that goes into the ISFR is forest cover mapping of the\ncountry based on nationwide forest cover mapping using satellite data. The forest\ncover is defined as “all lands, more than one hectare with a tree canopy density\nof more than or equal to 10% irrespective of ownership, legal status and land use.\nSuch lands may not necessarily be a recorded forest area. It also includes orchards,\nbamboo and palm”. In the current cycle, Forest Cover Mapping has been carried\nout using medium-resolution indigenous satellite data, with a spatial resolution of\n23.5 m sourced from the Indian Space Research Organization’s (ISRO) indigenous\nLISS-III sensor, part of the IRS Resourcesat satellite series, at a scale of 1: 50,000.\nThis satellite data was acquired for all states within the timeframe of October 2021\nto December 2021. In certain regions of the country, such as the North Eastern\nregion, the coastal belt, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, additional satellite\nimages were procured for the period from January 2022 to April 2022, to obtain\nbetter-quality satellite imagery. This specific time window was chosen because\nit typically offers cloud-free satellite data and full vegetation foliage, resulting in\nenhanced reflectance and precise satellite image interpretation.\n\nxiii\n\nThe classification of forest cover used in the present report is based on tree\ncanopy density, viz., Very Dense Forest (VDF) having canopy density equal to or\nmore than 70%, Moderately Dense Forest (MDF) having canopy density equal to\nor more than 40% but less than 70%, and Open Forest (OF) having canopy density\nequal to or more than 10% but less than 40%.\nThe Forest Cover is assessed using an approach involving satellite digital\nimage processing; visual image analysis; ground verification by the analysts and\nState Forest Departments; incorporation of post-field corrections; quality checks\nForest Survey of India\n\n\fincluding ground validation by officers; followed by generation of output in the\nform of maps and area statistics.\nOver the years, this methodology has continuously evolved and improved\nto keep pace with advancing technology and the latest image interpretation\ntechniques. Since the initial forest assessment report in 1987, the methodology\nfor Forest Cover Mapping has been consistently refined and updated. To ensure\nconsistency, uniformity, and a high level of accuracy in the Forest Cover Mapping\nexercise, all steps of the methodology have been standardized. To minimize\nsubjectivity, a comprehensive manual has been developed to guide and facilitate\nthese processes, helping to maintain the quality and reliability of the mapping\nresults.\nThe second major input that goes into ISFR is based on the inventory of\nForests and Trees Outside Forests (TOF) under the National Forest Inventory (NFI)\nProgramme of FSI. FSI launched a National Forest Inventory in 2002, with the\nonset of the 10th five-year plan, by developing a sampling design, to generate the\nnational level estimates of growing stock and other parameters. Under this NFI\ndesign, the country was stratified into 14 physiographic zones and 60 districts\nwere selected for the detailed inventory for a cycle of 2 years. About 3,500 sample\nplots were inventoried in the forest areas and 5000 sample plots were inventoried\nin TOF every year. FSI modified the sampling design of NFI in 2016, considering\nthe data requirements at National and International level, to generate the precise\nestimates at the State level and to reduce the revisit time from 20 years to 5 years.\nUnder the modified design, FSI has switched over to a grid based design having\nuniform grids of size 5 km x 5 km and selecting specified grids each year for the\ndetailed inventory. Under this design, FSI is laying about 6,000 plots in forest area\nand 10,000 plots in TOF areas every year. The information of growing stock, tree\ncover, bamboo stock, carbon stock, agroforestry and important characteristics are\nderived from the field inventory data collected from forest and TOF.\nThe ISFR 2023 has been produced into two volumes considering the wealth\nof information generated from forest cover mapping and NFI. The Volume-I gives\nthe national level assessment such as forest cover, mangrove cover, forest fires,\ngrowing stock, carbon stock, agroforestry, important characteristics of forest and\ndecadal change. The Volume-II gives information about forest cover for each\nState/UT of the country, districts and divisions and state wise information derived\nfrom the field inventory.\n\nThe key findings of the ISFR 2023 are as follows:\n• The total forest and tree cover of the country is 8,27,356.95 km2 which is\n25.17% of the geographical area of the country. The total Forest Cover has an area\nof 7,15,342.61 km2 (21.76%) whereas the Tree Cover has an area of 1,12,014.34\nkm2 (3.41%).\nForest Survey of India\n\nxiv\n\nSalient findings\n\n\fIndia State of Forest Report 2023 (Volume 1)\n\n• The current assessment shows an increase of 156.41 km2 in the Forest Cover\nat national level as compared to the previous assessment.\n• The total forest and tree cover of the country has increased by 1445.81 km2 as\ncompared to the last assessment of 2021.\n• The maximum increase in forest and tree cover has been observed in the\nStates of Chhattisgarh (683.62 km2) followed by Uttar Pradesh (559.19 km2), Odisha\n(558.57 km2) and Rajasthan (394.46 km2). The maximum decrease in forest and\ntree cover has been noticed in the state of Madhya Pradesh (612.41 km2) followed\nby Karnataka (459.36 km2), Ladakh (159.26 km2) and Nagaland (125.22 km2).\n• The States showing maximum increase of Forest Cover inside the RFA/GW are\nMizoram (192.92 km2) followed by Odisha (118.17 km2), Karnataka (93.14 km2),\nWest Bengal (64.79 km2) and Jharkhand (52.72 km2), whereas the States showing\nthe maximum decrease of Forest Cover inside the RFA/GW are Tripura (116.90 km2)\nfollowed by Telangana (105.87 km2), Assam (86.66 km2), Andhra Pradesh (83.47\nkm2) and Gujarat (61.22 km2).\n• The forest cover outside RFA has been shown maximum increase in the state\nof Gujarat (241.29 km2) followed by Bihar (106.85 km2), Kerala (95.19 km2), Uttar\nPradesh (79.27 km2) and Assam (74.90 km2). The states showing decrease in the\nforest cover outside RFA are Madhya Pradesh (344.77 km2) followed by Rajasthan\n(110.65 km2), Andhra Pradesh (55.19 km2), Arunachal Pradesh (45.32 km2) and\nMaharashtra (41.07 km2).\n• The extent of TOF (forest cover outside the RFA & GW and tree cover) has been\nfound to be 30.70 M ha, which is 37.11% of the total forest and tree cover in the\ncountry.\n• The maximum tree cover has been found in the State of Maharashtra\n(14,524.88 km2) followed by Rajasthan (10,841.12 km2) and Uttar Pradesh\n(8,950.92 km2). The maximum positive change as compared to ISFR 2021 has been\nobserved in Chhattisgarh (702.75 km2) followed by Rajasthan (478.26 km2) and\nUttar Pradesh (440.76 km2). In general, twenty-one States and UTs have shown an\nincreasing trend in tree cover, which indicates that agroforestry, is being promoted\nin these States\n\nxv\n\n• Western Ghats Eco-Sensitive Areas (WGESA) occupies an area of approximately\n60,285.61 km2 based on the digital boundary provided by MoEF & CC. Forest cover\nin all districts under WGESA has been estimated as 44,043.99 km2 (73%).\n• FSI has carried out a decadal changes analysis of forest cover of WGESA and\nobserved that there has been an overall loss of 58.22 km² in forest cover during the\nForest Survey of India\n\n\flast 10 years. Without water, life cannot exist; \nhence this vital resource should not be hampered or polluted. Water is one of \nthe most precious natural assets abound on the earth. Over 70% of the earth \nsurface is covered with water, which is a universal solvent essential for life. \nAll biological processes in cells take place in an aqueous medium; all reactions \nwithin cells between various substances occur between the substances that are \ndissolved  in  water.  The  availability  of  water  is  important  for  deciding  the \nnumber of individuals of each species that can survive in one particular area. \nIt is quite evident that diversity of life in any particular location is very much \ndecided by the availability of water there. Hence, it is an undeniable fact that \nwater is a vital resource because it by itself determines the life on earth. The \nterm 'pollution' generally refers to the addition of any foreign body or deletion \nof anything that naturally exists. Anything that causes hindrance to the usage \nof water by any form of life is termed as water pollution. The polluted water \nis either unsuitable or toxic to the kind of life that is existing in that area. All \nforms  of  life  on  earth  directly  or  indirectly  depend  upon  water  for  their \nsurvival. The major surface of the Earth’s surface is covered by water. All that \nwater exists in nature in various compartments of atmosphere and lithosphere, \nmaking it susceptible to pollution. The sources of water pollution are domestic \ndrainage and sanitary waste, industrial drainage and sewage, industrial waste \nfrom  factories,  dumping  of  domestic  garbage  on  on-land  bodies,  chemical \nrunoff  and  many  others.  Water  can  get  polluted  by  solid  particulates  in \nsuspension  and  also  by  dissolved  species  in  solution.  Pollution  can  be \nmanaged depending on the situation. The agents that cause pollution are called \npollutants.  They  include  organic,  inorganic,  and  biological  entities.  Water \npollution is a big issue that concerns humankind and other organisms. When \nthe  quality  of  water  used  is  progressively  diminished,  water  pollution  has \noccurred.  It  concerns  a  sum  of  things.  The  quality  of  water  utilized  and \nconsumed is an important factor that determines the welfare of living things. \nThis  can  be  ascertained  by  the  side  effects  of  contaminated  water.  The \nconsequence of this is waterborne diseases, affecting infections of people due \nto untreated health problems. Waterborne diseases are diseases that are caused \nby pathogens that enter the body through contaminated water. Some infections \noccur immediately, while it commonly takes time for pathogens to grow. \n\nPage | 1 \n\n \n \n\fChapter - 1 \n\nIntroduction to Water Pollution \n\nWater is absolutely essential for the sustenance and proper functioning of all \nliving organisms on the earth, playing an irreplaceable role in the continuity \nThe PDF <_io.BufferedReader name='/environment/input_artifacts/Pollution.pdf'> contains a metadata field indicating that it should not allow text extraction. The first and foremost requirement, therefore, was to undertake systematic\naerial surveys of our forests, and prepare an inventory of the forest resources. This\nexercise started with a limited mandate of conducting a survey to assess availability\nof commercial wood to establish forest produce based industries. The ‘Pre-Investment\nSurvey of Forest Resources’ (PISFR) was, thus, established in 1965 as an FAO/UNDP/\nGOI project. The scope of PISFR’s activities was expanded and it was re-organized as the\nForest Survey of India (FSI) in 1981. FSI has come a long way since then, and now offers\nvarious services, including forest resource assessment, forest cover mapping, forest\ninventory, e-green watch, decision support system, and forest fire monitoring.\n\nIndia State of Forest Report 1.2\nOne of the major tasks assigned to FSI is to publish the biennial India State of Forests\nReport (ISFR). This report is the 18th report in this series. The ISFR stands as a testament\nto our nation’s commitment towards the conservation and sustainable management\nof our invaluable forest resources. This report is not merely a compendium of statistics,\nbut a chronicle of our collective efforts, an appraisal of challenges faced, and a blueprint\nfor the future. It embodies the tireless work of foresters, conservationists, scientists,\nand communities who have dedicated themselves to the cause of forest conservation.\nIt speaks of an evolving narrative of environmental stewardship, shaped by policies,\nscientific advancements, and the indefatigable spirit of those who believe in the sanctity\nof our forests.\nPrimary objective of the ISFR 2023 is to present an in-depth analysis of the current\nstatus of forests in India, providing critical insights into the health, extent, and distribution\nof forested areas. It definitely provides information on the results of our Forest\nManagement practices. It aims to serve as a valuable resource for practicing foresters,\npolicymakers, researchers, conservationists, and the public, fostering a holistic under-\n\n1.1\n\n\fIndia State of Forest Report 2023 (Volume 1)\n\nstanding of the challenges and opportunities surrounding forest management and\nbiodiversity conservation.\nThe report draws upon a robust and multi-faceted methodology, integrating remote\nsensing technology, ground surveys, and advanced data analytics. This triangulation\nof methods ensures accuracy, reliability, and comprehensiveness in the assessment of\nforest cover, type, and quality across the Indian landscape.\nIndia has made significant commitments to various global treaties and initiatives\nrelated to forests, climate change, sustainable development, biodiversity, mangroves,\nand landscape restoration. These commitments necessitate reporting of the state of\ncountry’s forests on a periodic basis. Some of the relevant commitments include the\nfollowing:\n1.\n\nUnited Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)\n\nThe UNFCCC is an international treaty aimed at addressing climate change and its\nimpacts. India is a party to this convention, which requires member countries to\nreport on their greenhouse gas emissions, as well as activities related to land use,\nland-use change, and forestry (LULUCF).\n2.\n\nKyoto Protocol\n\nThe Kyoto Protocol operationalizes the UNFCCC by committing industrialized\ncountries and economies in transition to limit and reduce greenhouse gases\n(GHG) emissions in accordance with agreed individual targets.\n3.\n\nParis Agreement\n\nParis Agreement, under the UNFCCC, sets out ambitious goals to limit global\nwarming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and to pursue\nefforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees Celsius. It emphasizes the importance of forests\nin climate mitigation and adaptation strategies.\n4.\n\nSustainable Development Goals (SDG)\n\n4\n\nThe 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by all United Nations\nmembers in 2015, created 17 world Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The\nSDG 15: “Life on Land”, specifically targets the conservation, restoration, and\nsustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, including forests. The SDG 14 “Life\nbelow Water” seeks to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine\nresources for sustainable development. Targets 14.2.1, 14.5.2, 15.1.1, 15.1.2.,\n15.2.1, 15.2.3, 15.3.2, and 15.4.1 are directly relevant to Forest Statistics. Besides,\nSDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being),\nSDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), and SDG 13 (Climate Action) are also relevant\nto the Forestry sector.\n\nForest Survey of India\n\n\fIntroduction\n\n5.\n\nConvention on Biological Diversity (CBD)\n\nThe CBD aims to conserve biological diversity, ensure sustainable use of its\ncomponents, and promote fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic\nresources. India, being a party to the CBD, is obligated to report on its efforts in\nconserving biodiversity, which includes forest ecosystems. The Aichi Biodiversity\nTargets have been established under the CBD to guide international efforts in\nbiodiversity conservation. Aichi Target 5 specifically addresses the conservation of\nhabitats, including forests.\n6.\n\nNew York Declaration on Forests (NYDF)\n\nNYDF is a voluntary international declaration that aims to halve deforestation by\n2020 and end it by 2030, while also restoring forests and enhancing sustainable\nmanagement.\n7.\n\nUnited Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD)\n\nEstablished in 1994, UNCCD is a legally binding convention that links development\nand environment to sustainable land management. The convention aims to combat\ndesertification and the ill effects of drought.\n8.\n\nBonn Challenge\n\nBonn Challenge is a global effort to bring under restoration 150 million hectares\nof the world’s deforested and degraded lands by 2020, and 350 million hectares by\n2030. India has made commitment of bringing 26 million ha under this initiative to\nrestore degraded landscapes. UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021-2030)\ncalls for the scaling up of efforts to restore ecosystems and combat climate change,\nand India is a participant in this global initiative also.\n9.\n\nAsia Pacific Forestry Commission (APFC)\n\nIndia, as a member of APFC, is part of a regional body that aims to promote sustainable\nforest management in the Asia-Pacific region. Reporting on the state of forests is an\nintegral part of this endeavour.\n10. Ramsar Convention on Wetlands\n\nThese commitments collectively highlight India’s obligation to monitor, report, and\ntake action on the state of its forests in the context of global efforts towards climate\nchange mitigation, landscape restoration, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable\ndevelopment. These underscore India’s role as a responsible stakeholder in the\ninternational community’s efforts towards environmental conservation and sustainable\ndevelopment.\nForest Survey of India\n\n5\n\nIndia is a party to the Ramsar Convention, which recognizes the importance of\nwetlands, including mangroves, and commits to their conservation and sustainable\nuse.\n\n\fIndia State of Forest Report 2023 (Volume 1)\n\nThe India State of Forest Reports contribute towards all these goals, setting reporting\nbenchmarks every two years.\n\n1.3 Technology Advancements in Forest Resource\nAssessment\nOver the years, several technological and methodological advances have significantly\nimproved the forest cover mapping conducted by FSI. hectare in area, with a tree canopy of more than or equal\nto 10%, irrespective of ownership and legal status; and includes orchards, bamboo,\nand palm. Thus, ‘Forest cover’ indicates presence of trees on any land, irrespective of\nownership of land; and irrespective of the fact whether the land is notified as a forest\nland or not. It is not possible for FSI to distinguish a tree clad area on the basis of legal\nstatus of land using the remote sensing techniques. Hence, the ‘forest cover’ data, as\ncaptured and analysed using satellite imageries, is reported as such.\n\n1.5.2 Recorded Forest Area\nThe ‘recorded forest area’ (RFA) (or forest area) refers to all the geographic area\nrecorded as ‘forest’ in government records. The ‘recorded forest area’ largely consists\nof the ‘Reserved Forests’ (RF) and the ‘Protected Forests’ (PF), constituted under the\nprovisions of the Indian Forest Act, 1927. Besides the RFs and PFs, the recorded forest\narea may also include all such areas which have been recorded as ‘Unclassed Forests’,\n‘Village Forests’, or by any other nomenclature of such description, and all such areas\nwhich have been recorded as forest in the revenue records, or have been constituted\nso under any State Act or local law. A recorded forest area may, or may not, have tree\ncover. Besides being richly forested, recorded forest areas may have less than 10%\ncanopy cover, pastures, desert lands, blanks, wetland, rivers, riverbeds, creeks, snow\nclad areas, etc. FSI obtains the information about the RFA from the respective State/\nUT Governments, as they are the custodians of this information.\nFor the purpose of this report, ‘tree cover’ refers to the area covered by trees outside\nrecorded forest areas. These areas range from that covered by a single tree to patches\nof trees less than 1 ha, as areas more than 1 ha are already covered in the Forest\ncover. Such small patches may comprise of bock plantations, linear plantations, and\nscattered trees not delineated as forest cover during interpretation of satellite data.\nForest Survey of And\nis the situation really this grim? Is it time to start shedding bitter tears, or is\nthere something we can do to control environmental pollution?\nThe objective of this book is to at least begin to answer these questions. As\nthe title suggests, this book focuses first on the problems of environmental pol-\nlution, but then concentrates on methods of control--what we humans can do\nto prevent and control the pollution of our planet.\nWe define environmental pollution as the contamination of air, water, or\nfood in such a manner as to cause real or potential harm to human health or\nwell-being, or to damage or harm nonhuman nature without justification. The\nquestion of when harm to nonhuman nature is justified is a sticky one and is\naddressed below in the discussion on ethics.\nIn this first chapter we begin by asking why we seem to have such prob-\nlems with environmental pollution. Where do these problems originate, and\nwhat or who is to blame for what many consider to be the sorry state of the\nworld? Next we discuss our environmental problems within the framework of\nethics. We begin by showing how the most basic concepts of environmental pol-\nlution that reflect public health concerns are really ethical issues. We then dis-\ncuss how these ethics have been used to extend the concerns with pollution\nbeyond public health to include the despoliation of the planet, including the ex-\ntinction of species and destruction of places. All of these problems are still\nwithin the context of harm to humans. Finally, we discuss issues that have noth-\ning to do with public health or human well-being, but nevertheless are impor-\ntant to us in terms of environmental quality.\n\n--- Page 7 ---\n2 ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND CONTROL\n,llEI\nl!lt\n/\n_~ ,.-v-_~-_\nm\nFIGURE 1-1. Human excreta disposal, from an old woodcut. [Source: Reyburn, W.,\nFlushed with Pride, London: McDonald (1969).]\nTHE ROOTS OF OUR ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS\nMuch of the history of Western civilizations has been characterized as ex-\nploitation, destruction, and noncaring for the environment. Why are we such a\ndestructive species? Various arguments have been advanced to explain the roots\nof our environmentally destructive tendencies, including our religions, our so-\ncial and economic structure, and our acceptance of technology.\nReligion. In the first chapter of Genesis, people are commanded by God to sub-\ndue nature, to procreate, and to have dominion over all living things. This an-\nthropocentric view of nature runs through the Judaeo-Christian doctrine,\nplacing humans at the pinnacle of development and encouraging humans to use\nnature as we see fit.\nIn his essay, \"The Historical Roots of Our Ecological Crisis,\" Lynn White\nargues that those who embrace the Judaeo-Christian religions are taught to\n\n--- Page 8 ---\nPollution and Environmental Ethics 3\ntreat nature as an enemy and that natural resources are to be used to meet the\ngoals of human survival and propagation. From this dogma (so goes the argu-\nment) have developed technology and capitalistic economy, and, ultimately, en-\nvironmental degradation.\nBecause the Judaeo-Christian traditions are most prominent in the United\nStates, we often forget that this is not a majority religious tradition in the\nworld. Billions of people embrace very different deities and dogmas, and yet\nthey also live in capitalistic economies with perhaps even greater destruction of\nenvironmental quality. So it cannot be just the Judaeo-Christian religions that\nare to blame.\nRemember also that Christianity and Islam both developed at a time when\nthere were a number of competing religions from which to choose. For many,\nthe Christian ideas and ethics derived from the Judaic traditions seemed to fit\nmost comfortably with their existing ethics and value systems, while others\nchose Islam over other religions. It seems quite obvious that Christianity was\nnot the reason for the development of science, capitalism, and democracy, but\nsimply provided an ethical environment in which they flourished (at least in Eu-\nrope). It seems farfetched, therefore, to blame our environmental problems on\nour religions.\nSocial and Economic Structures. Perhaps it is our social structures that are re-\nsponsible for environmental degradation. Garrett Hardin's \"The Tragedy of the\nCommons\" illustrates this proposition with the following story: 1\nA village has a common green for the grazing of cattle, and the green is sur-\nrounded by farmhouses. Initially, each farmer has one cow, and the green can\neasily support the herd. Each farmer realizes, however, that if he or she gets\nanother cow, the cost of the additional cow to the farmer is negligible because\nthe cost of maintaining the green is shared, but the profits are the farmer's alone.\nSo one farmer gets more cows and reaps more profits, until the common green\ncan no longer support anyone's cows, and the system collapses.\nHardin presents this as a parable for overpopulation of the earth and conse-\nquent resource depletion. The social structure in the parable is capitalism--the\nindividual ownership of wealth--and the use of that wealth to serve selfish in-\nterests. Does that mean that noncapitalist economies (the totally and partially\nplanned economies) do a better job of environmental protection, natural re-\nsource p\n\n--- Page 9 ---\n4 ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND CONTROL\nsystem, production was the single goal and environmental degradation became\nunimportant. Also, there was no such thing as \"public opinion,\" of course, and\nhence nobody spoke up for the environment. When production in a centrally\ncontrolled economy is the goal, all life, including human life, is cheap and ex-\npendable. 2\nSome less industrialized societies, such as some Native American tribes, the\nFinno-Ugric people of northern Europe, and the Pennsylvania Amish in the\nUnited States, have developed a quasi-steady-state condition. These sociopo-\nlitical systems incorporate animistic religion, holding that nature contains spir-\nits that are powerful, sometimes friendly, and with whom bargains can be\nstruck. This\nmouse-shaft (hiirevihk) did not appear to have religious significance; it was ex-\nplained as a means of assuring the mice of their share of the harvest. 4\nThese societies were not all environmentally stable, however, nor did they de-\nliberately act to protect their environment. Those that are still in existence coex-\nist with the industrialized societies that have not achieved a steady state, use the\nproducts and marketing mechanisms of those states, and lose their young people\nto societies where there is wider opportunity. Society is the reflection of the needs\nand aspirations of the people who establish and maintain it. Had we not observed and been\nable to quantify phenomena like species endangerment and destruction, the ef-\nfect of herbicides and pesticides on wildlife, the destruction of the stratospheric\nozone layer, and fish kills due to water pollution, we would not even have re-\nalized what was happening to the world. Modern technology, however, not only\nprovides water and air treatment systems, but continues to develop ways in\nwhich to use a dwindling natural resource base more conservatively. Before  the  19th  century  industrial  revolution,  people  lived  in  harmony  with \n\ntheir  immediate  environment.  As  the  industrialization  has  spread  around  the  globe,  the \n\nproblem of water pollution has intensified. Today with over 8 billion people on the planet, the \n\npressure  on  the  water  resources  has  increased  and  water  pollution  has  become  an  emerging \n\nthreat.  In order to combat water pollution we must understand the problems associated with \n\nwater  pollution  and  become  the  part  of  the  solution.  In  this  context  the  course  Aquatic \n\nPollution  and  Coastal  Zone  Management  has  been  designed  to  expose  the  under  graduate \n\nstudents  of  Fisheries  Science  to  various  dimensions  of  Aquatic  Pollution,  resulting \n\nEnvironmental  and  Public  Health  Hazards  and  various  tools  available  for  monitoring  and \n\nabatement  of pollution. In addition,  the coastal ecosystems  which are highly productive and \n\nrich  in  biodiversity  has  been  explained.  The  course  Aquatic  Pollution  and  Coastal  Zone \n\nManagement has been divided into two parts. The first part covers Aquatic Pollution and the \n\nsecond part Coastal Zone Management. \n\nClassification of aquatic pollution \n\nPollution \n\nPollution is  defined as an undesirable  change in  the physical,  chemical  or biological \n\ncharacteristics of the environment, which can harmfully affect the health, survival or activities \n\nof  humans  or  other  living  organisms.  Environmental  pollution  is  an  emerging  threat  and  of \n\ngreat  concern in  today's  context  pertaining to  its effect  on the ecosystem. The technological \n\ndevelopments  in  agriculture,  industries  and  related  fields  have  resulted  in  unlimited \n\nexploitation of natural resources disturbing the delicate ecological balance between the living \n\nand nonliving components of the biosphere. \n\nMarine Pollution  \n\nGESAMP defined marine pollution as \"introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of \n\nsubstances  or  energy  into  the  marine  environment  (including  estuaries)  resulting  in  such \n\ndeleterious effects as harm to living resources, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine \n\n \n\factivities  including  fishing,  impairment  of  quality  for  use  of  sea-water,  and  reduction  of \n\namenities. \n\nGESAMP  (Group  of  Experts  on  the  Scientific  Aspects  of  Marine  Environmental \n\nProtection) is a group of experts that since 1969 has advised the United Nations system on \n\nscientific aspects of marine environmental protection. GESAMP is presently sponsored by ten \n\nUN agencies with interests and responsibilities in marine environmental matters: IMO, FAO, \n\nUNESCO-IOC,  WMO,  IAEA,  UN,  UN  Environment,  UNIDO,  UNDP  and  ISA.  This  joint \n\nadvisory mechanism is needed first to provide a cross-sectoral, interdisciplinary, and science-\n\nbased  approach  to  international  policy  development  in  marine  environmental  affairs,  and \n\nsecond  to  meet  the  practical  requirement  for  coordination  and  cooperation  among  UN \n\nagencies. \n\nPollutant  \n\nPollutant is  a  substance  that  pollutes  the  air,  water  or  land.  This  term  is  used  to \n\ndescribe things in the environment that do not belong. In a broader sense, the term 'pollutant' \n\nhas even been used to  describe undesirable levels of sound or light.  For example, the lights \n\nand  never-ending  traffic  noise  on  the  Las  Vegas  Strip  are  examples  of  light  and  noise \n\npollutants. \n\nDifficulties on Pollution Measurement  \n\nNatural  levels  of  most  contaminants  are  unknown  Pollutant  effects  can  be  complex \n\nand  take  a  long  time  to  develop  Pollutants  enter  into  aquatic  environment  through  a  great \n\nvariety of mechanisms The number of compounds that humans introduce into the ocean is so \n\nenormous, it will be difficult to track. \n\nClassification of Aquatic Pollution \n\n  Aquatic  pollution  can  be  classified  mainly  into  three  categories. Physical pollution is what you might refer to as trash and is the direct result of \n\nhuman actions. While  using  sludge-drying  beds  is  the \n\nmost  common  way  to  carry  out  this  process,  it  is  extremely  time-consuming  and  may  take \n\nweeks before the process is complete. In order to quicken these processes, waste management \n\nplans  are  also  employing solid-liquid  separation  devices to  carry  out  this  process. ---\nPreface\nMost individuals today are more conscious of their environment than in\nthe past and they are interested especially in those factors that degrade the\nenvironment. Mining is one of those factors. Mining refers to the process\nofextraction or abstraction of mineral deposits from either the surface of the\nEarth or from beneath the surface. In this context it also involves the abstrac-\ntion of oil, gas, water and brine from the ground. Furthermore, mining repre-\nsents one of man’s earliest activities reaching back into Palaeolithic times and,\nas such, has played an important role in the development of civilization. It is\nalso an activity that has and is going on more or less worldwide. With time,\nthe use of minerals has increased in both volume and variety in order to meet\na greater range of purposes and demand by society. Accordingly, present day\nsociety is more dependent on the minerals industry than in the past. Indeed,\nthe exploitation of minerals is fundamental to society now and will continue\nto be in the future. In other words, the mining of minerals contributes to the\nsustained economic progress of developed nations and helps to alleviate\npoverty and improve the quality of life of people in developing countries.\nFirst, mineral deposits have to be located, they then are worked and\nsubsequently processed. It is the working and processing of mineral\ndeposits that can give rise to environmental damage. This can mean that\nland is disturbed, that the topography is changed and that the hydrogeo-\nlogical conditions are affected adversely. The degree of impact that mining\nhas on the environment varies depending on the mineral worked, the\nmethod of working, and the location and size of the working. However,\nland that has become spoiled by past mining activity generally can be reha-\nbilitated but at a cost. This cost may be recovered indirectly by the benefit\nthat a more attractive environment brings to the area so affected. In order\nto rehabilitate land that has been affected adversely by mining activity, the\nsite or area concerned has to be investigated before it can be treated.\nConsequently, the primary objective of this book is to provide an\noverview of various aspects of mining and how they affect the surrounding\nenvironment, and, just as importantly, how the arising environmental\nproblems can be investigated and subsequently dealt with. Hopefully, this\nshould enable the hazard liabilities from mining and their associated risks to\n\n--- Page 11 ---\nx Preface\nbe assessed more readily. As such, it is hoped that this book will be of value\nto those who are involved with the development or redevelopment of min-\ning areas. These include civil engineers, mining engineers, geotechnical engi-\nneers, engineering geologists, mining geologists, environmental scientists and\nmanagers, hydrologists and hydrogeologists, utilities engineers, builders,\nmineral surveyors, conveyance lawyers, insurance officers, land owners and\nplanners. Although it has been attempted to give a broad overview of the\nsubject this, no doubt, has been influenced by the experience of the authors\nso that it may reflect a certain bias. Case histories have been provided at the\nend of each chapter, except that of the Introduction. These generally illus-\ntrate the content of the individual chapter but in someinstances go further\nand introduce new material. Numerous references have been provided to\nhelp allow the reader to pursue his/her interests further.\nAs far as the authors are aware, there is no book available today that is\nsimilar to this in content. In other words, no book provides a survey, in par-\nticular, of various aspects of subsidence, of waste disposal, of pollution and\nof dereliction as caused by different types of mining, and their investigation\nand treatment. In addition, topics such as spontaneous combustion, gases\nand induced seismicity also are included within the text. Nonetheless, not\nevery aspect of environmental degradation such as noise and dust is cov-\nered. This primarily is because of the limitations of the author’s experience.\nThe authors would like to express their thanks to various individuals and\norganizations for the help provided during the production of this book. In\nparticular, they would like to thank Professor Dick Stacey, Mr Howard\nSiddle, Mr John Sinclair, Dr John Cripps, Dr David Reddish, Dr Dave\nButtrick, Mr Roy Piggott, Mr Ross Parry-Davies, Mrs Susan Mills, the\nHalcrow Group Limited, the British Geological Survey, International Mining\nConsultants Limited, the Coal Authority, Anglo American Plc, Infoterra\nLimited, White Young Green Consulting Limited, the Canadian Geotechnical\nSociety, the United States Department of the Interior, the International\nAssociation of Hydrological Sciences, the United States Geological Survey,\nthe United States Bureau of Mines, SRK Consulting South Africa, Thomas\nTelford Publishing, the Institution of Civil Engineers, the International\nSociety for Soil Mechanics and Geotechni\n\n--- Page 12 ---\nChapter 1\nIntroduction\n1.1. Introduction\nMining, alongside agriculture, represents one of man’s earliest activities, the\ntwo being fundamental to the development and continuation of civilization.\nIn fact, the oldest known mine in the archaeological record is the Lion Cave\nin Swaziland, which has a radio carbon age of 43000 years. There\nPalaeolithic humans mined hematite, which they presumably ground to\nproduce the red pigment ochre. Moreover, the dependence of primitive\nsocieties on mined products is illustrated by the terms Stone Age, Bronze\nAge and Iron Age, a sequence of ages that indicate the increasing complex-\nity of the relationship between mining and society. In order to produce a\nflint axe meant that a suitable deposit of flint had to be located, that a\nmethod of mining be developed that would allow the flint to be worked,\nand that a means of processing be evolved to fashion the flint into a finished\nproduct. These requirements are more or less the same for mineral produc-\ntion at the present time. This general sequence applied in the Bronze and\nIron Ages but the processing in particular became more sophisticated. With\ntime, the use of minerals has increased in both volume and variety in order\nto meet a greater range of purposes and demand by society, and the means\nof locating, working and processing minerals has increased in complexity.\nToday, society is even more dependent on the minerals industry than in the\npast. In fact, it can be claimed that every material thing in society is either\ndirectly derived from a mineral product or is produced with the aid of min-\neral derivatives such as steel, energy or fertilizers. The importance of the\nminerals industry therefore cannot be overstressed.\nHowever, unlike agriculture where there is some choice in where and\nwhat to grow, mining can only take place where minerals are present and\neconomically viable to work. The localized nature of mineral deposits,\nasopposed to the widespread demand for them, led to the development of\ntrade between peoples from prehistoric times onwards. The desire\ntoacquire minerals, notably precious minerals, has led to exploration of far\noff lands, to wars and to conquest. Another important aspect of mining is\n\n--- Page 13 ---\n2 Introduction\nthat it is a robber economy, in that a mineral deposit is a finite resource and\nso mining comes to an end when the mineral deposit is exhausted or\nbecomes uneconomic to mine or abstract. Perhaps groundwater abstraction\nis the exception in that with proper management it should be sustainable.\nDeposits that are abandoned when they become uneconomic to work may\nbe reworked at some time in the future when mining technology or demand\nmakes their exploitation once again worthwhile.\nMining, and associated mineral processing and beneficiation, does\nimpact on the environment. Unfortunately, this frequently has led to\nserious consequences. The impact of mining depends on many factors,\nespecially the type of mining and the size of the operation. It can mean that\nland is disturbed, that the topography is changed and that the hydro-\ngeological conditions are affected adversely. Mining also has social impacts\non the environment. Communities grow up around mines. When the mines\nclose, the communities can suffer and even may die, becoming ‘ghost\ntowns’.\nIn the past the mining industry frequently showed a lack of concern for\nthe environment. This does not necessarily imply that society was not aware\nof the environmental problems that could be associated with mining. For\ninstance, in 1306 a royal proclamation prohibited the use of coal in London\nfor domestic and industrial purposes because of the nuisance caused by\nsmoke but it proved impossible to enforce. In addition, Agricola (1556)\nreferred to environmental problems created by mining such as the devasta-\ntion of fields and the pollution of streams. What is more, as technology has\ndeveloped, so mining has had an increasing impact on the environment. The\ndisposal of waste, in particular, has led to unsightly spoils being left to\ndisfigure the landscape, and to surface streams and groundwater being\npolluted. Urban areas have suffered serious subsidence damage by under-\nmining. Today, however, the greater awareness of the importance of the\nenvironment has led to tighter legislation being imposed by many countries\nto lessen the impact of mining. This is especially the case in the developed,\nmore affluent nations. Unfortunately, many poorer countries, in which the\nprimary minerals industry is proportionately of greater economic impor-\ntance, are reluctant to impose non-essential restrictions on their principal\nearners of wealth and foreign exchange. What is more, the concept of\nreclamation of a site after minin\n\n--- Page 14 ---\nIntroduction 3\nhowever, are a local phenomena, although they may impact beyond\nmine boundaries. They also account for only a small part of the land area\nof a country (e.g. the mining industry accounts for less than 1% of the total\narea of South Africa). Land that has become derelict by past mining activ-\nity can be reclaimed. Rehabilitated spoil heaps frequently become centres of\nsocial amenity such as parklands, golf courses and even artificial ski slopes.\nOpen-pits, when they fill with water, can be used as marinas, for fishing or\nas wildlife reserves. Even some underground mines can be used, such as\nthose in limestone at Kansas City, Missouri, which are used as warehouses,\ncold storage facilities and offices (Fig.1.1). Mining therefore can be looked\nupon as one of the stages in the sequential use of land.\nFigure 1.1 An entrance to old workings in the Bethaney Falls Limestone,Kansas City,\nUnited States,which are now used for warehousing,cold storage etc.\n\n--- Page 15 ---\n4 Introduction\n1.2. Environmental problems and impacts\nMining may be regarded as the removal of minerals, in solid, liquid or\ngaseous form, from the Earth’s crust for use in the service of society.\nIttherefore involves exploration for and exploitation of mineral deposits by\nsurface or underground methods. Accordingly, mining inevitably brings\nabout change to the environment and so has an environmental impact. The\ndegree of impact can vary from more or less imperceptible to highly intru-\nsive and depends on the mineral worked, the method of working, and the\nlocation and size of the mine. Unfortunately, there is no consistent means\nby which to quantitatively assess some environmental impacts, notably\nthose of a visual nature, so that any assessment of such impact tends to be\nqualitative with an appreciable element of subjectivity. On the other hand,\nsome impacts can be quantitatively assessed such as the degree to which\ngroundwater has been polluted. Obviously, the most severe environmental\nimpacts occur where mining is going or has gone on, the effect of the impact\nreducing with increasing distance from the mine responsible.\nMining can pose a direct hazard to humans, apart from mine employees.\nFortunately, mining hazards only infrequently lead to death or serious\ninjury. Nonetheless, there are instances when, for example, old partially\nsealed shafts have opened beneath people who then have fallen to their\ndeath, where tailings dams have burst and killed people or where spoil heaps\nhave failed causing death. Effluents from mines and mine wastes may be\ntoxic and kill vegetation, and injure animals. Water pollution can continue\nfor a long period after the mine causing the problem has ceased operation\nand as such can pose a health hazard. Many aspects of mining have the\npotential to cause damage to land and property, and thereby represent a\ndirect financial loss to those affected. Admittedly, compensation can be paid\nto those affected but this may involve contentious legal disputes.\nLoss of amenity or nuisance frequently is associated with mining but this\ndoes not necessarily threaten human life, although adversely affecting the\nquality of life. In some instances, this may be difficult to quantity whilst in\nothers such as blasting it is possible to recognize and so assess levels of nui-\nsance below the threshold of damage. Even so, the nuisance caused by blast-\ning depends upon a number of factors such as intensity, frequency,\nduration, time of day, human susce\n\n--- Page 557 ---\n546 Index\nPolycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons Sinkholes 9, 38, 116, 229–231, 232,\n(PAHs) 451 235, 236, 238, 239, 246, 277–278,\nPorcupine technique 192, 194 382; It crosses boundaries of space and time, recurs in\nall human communities and finds expression in every aspect of cultural\nproduction – from pre-historic cave paintings to high-tech computer games.\nThis volume examines historical and imaginary scenarios of apocalypse, the\ndepiction of its likely triggers, and imagined landscapes in the aftermath\nof global destruction. Its discussion moves effortlessly from classic novels\nincluding Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World, George Orwell’s Nineteen\nEighty-Four and Margaret Atwood’s Oryx and Crake, to blockbuster films\nsuch as Blade Runner, Armageddon and Invasion of the Body Snatchers.\nLisboa also takes into account religious doctrine, scientific research and the\nvisual arts to create a penetrating, multi-disciplinary study that provides\nprofound insight into one of Western culture’s most fascinating and\nenduring preoccupations.\nAs with all Open Book publications the entire work is available free to\nread online, while printable digital editions of the volume together with\nadditional resources can be downloaded from the publisher’s website:\nwww.openbookpublishers.com\nOpenBook\nPublishers\nKnowledge is for sharing\n","message":"Command executed successfully.","display":[],"extras":null}}}}}}
